#5732. EVs Displace 5 Times More Oil Globally Than They Did 5 Years Ago — Analysis

Five years on from Glasgow, EVs have proved the single most effective way to curb oil use, says T&E.

At COP26 in Glasgow, twenty-four countries and a group of leading car manufacturers committed to ending the era of fossil-fuel powered vehicles by 2040 “or earlier”. Five years and two energy crises later, oil savings from EVs globally are up fivefold, new T&E analysis shows. EVs are the single most effective way of cutting oil demand, improving energy security and reducing emissions, says T&E.

While battery electric vehicles (BEVs) represent just 4.2% of the global fleet, they now account for 25% of all new car sales worldwide – up from 6.6% five years ago. This surge has pushed oil displacement from 215,000 barrels a day in 2021 to 1.2 million barrels a day today, or roughly 1.2% of global consumption.

At the same time, electric buses now make up 5% of the global fleet, battery electric trucks are at 1% but in some countries exceed 50% of new sales. T&E estimates these vehicles avoid as much as 320,000 barrels a day. As road transport burns close to half of all the world’s oil, transitioning to EVs is crucial in reducing oil dependency. As the global car and truck fleet continues to grow, EVs are the only thing stopping runaway oil demand, warns T&E.

As electrification takes center stage at this year’s COP, current policies put battery electric cars on track to displace roughly 5.8 million barrels of oil a day by 2034 — matching the sustained disruption seen during the 2026 crisis. Accelerating EV adoption will be crucial to preventing future oil shocks, according to T&E.

Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E, said: “Electric vehicles are the single most effective way of cutting oil demand. Right now the only winners in our oil addiction are fossil fuel giants and petrostates. Places with near 100% sales of EVs like Norway, Denmark and Hong Kong have effectively insulated themselves from future shocks. Five years after Glasgow, EVs stand as one of the clearest victories in global climate history. At this year’s COP, world leaders must set binding electrification targets. Not just for the climate, but for national security.”

BEVs on the road now avoid more than 200 Mt of CO2-equivalent a year. According to T&E, rapid transport electrification is a vital part of the wider energy transition by providing essential grid flexibility and storage. Just as past COPs accelerated the global boom in wind and solar, backing for electric vehicles at COP31 can deliver the same breakthrough, slashing oil demand and driving emissions down.

[1] Displaced oil is estimated from daily per vehicle savings: about 0.019 barrels per car (derived from Ember), 0.2 per truck (IEA) and 0.15 per bus (bottom-up from typical fuel use and mileage). The 2026 supply loss has been estimated at 5.8 million barrels a day. We use IEA fleet projections for 2030 and 2035 fleet sizes to calculate the offset year of the BEV car fleet. Results exclude plug-in hybrids, vans and two- and three-wheelers.

For the chart, global capacity and generation for up to 2024 come from the US EIA. For 2025, we used IRENA capacity additions and Ember generation data. Values for 2026 are T&E estimates based on Chinese installation data to September 2026 and generation on IEA mid-year growth forecasts. Global BEV sales from Ember.

#5731. IIHS Founder Warned Drivers About The Dangers Of Speed Almost A Decade Before He Started The Organization: What's Streaming

Not long before the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety was informing drivers of how dangerous or safe a car was, James S. Kemper was on a mission to improve road safety. Kemper worked in the insurance world in his first job out of high school. He was an "office boy" for Central Mutual Insurance according to his New York Times obituary, but he went on to produce his own driver safety materials: educational films.

The films were made by Kemper's personal insurance company, Lumbermen Mutual Casualty, and in partnership with the LAPD and Traffic Safety Films Inc. The LAPD connection helped bring "Sergeant Bruce" to the films, who starred on-camera several times as the presenter of important safety lessons — each video with its own specific theme. Maybe it's Sgt. Bruce's personality, or maybe it's a cop-thing, but he also delivers a pseudo 1950s-version of scared straight energy with every specific dangerous driving situation.

Join me as I introduce a new(er), sometimes nostalgic video worth adding to your Watch Later lists. Leave a note in the comments if you find an older or interesting film you'd like to see featured.

In "Speed, The Accident Multiplier," a film restored and posted by 16mm Time Machine on YouTube, the on-camera narrator, Sergeant Bruce of the LAPD, explains to viewers that speed is dangerous. He uses charts and figures to show how faster speed increases stopping distances. The biggest takeaway is that the faster you go, the longer it takes to brake, and the more likely the damage to whatever the car hits will be catastrophic. That same messaging carried over into the IIHS organization decades later.

Sgt. Bruce ended the film in a familiar way that you'll find with most of these films: A message about how engaging with these dangers will lead to death. In "Speed," he tells viewers, "Speeding is a two-edged sword. It makes an accident more probable, and at the same time, it makes death more certain." He went on to explain that one out of every three fatal accidents involved a speeding driver, "which means in one out of three cases, a driver took a chance with death and lost."

There are a couple more films Kemper and his organizations had made in 1950 that are also available on YouTube. The next two, or rather four, were uploaded by PeriscopeFilm — specifically, they're two short double-features. The first pairs "Following Too Close" and "Driver Irritations," with the second pairing including "Child Safety" and "Driver or Pedestrian" — with the latter admittedly sounding more like a dangerous game, and that was likely the point. The opening to "Driver or Pedestrian" doesn't mess around either. Within the first minute, a camera follows a man driving a car as Sgt. Bruce tells viewers, "This is a driver..." before cutting to a tombstone, where Sgt. Bruce adds, "...who was a pedestrian. This is how it happened." Quite a way to set the scene.

Nine years later, Kemper's company joined forces with another two insurance companies to form the IIHS. Another decade after that, the IIHS would become its own scientific research organization, conducting studies to better understand road safety and finding ways to help improve it. By that point, IIHS had begun to do its own vehicle safety testing, as well. Those tests — although they have changed some as vehicles have evolved quite a bit since the 1960s — still provide consumers with important information regarding the safety of their vehicles today, like its latest look into the safety of heavy-duty trucks and cargo vans.

Kemper's work in insurance also helped push mutual insurance to the forefront in the U.S., which, if you're unfamiliar, it means the insurance company is owned by policyholders. There are no stock shareholders to appease. He was adamant about ensuring people were paid for their claims. In his New York Times obituary, he's quoted saying, "I made up my mind that this company was going to settle claims for cash in the shortest time possible. I did not see then and do not see now the value of contesting claims you know you will settle." Anyone feel like a few insurance companies could take some notes? Kemper's legacy endures with his insurance company over a century later, which now exists as Kemper Insurance, and the place where he left the biggest mark — in his role establishing the IIHS.

#5729. Nanobody Shows Promise in Myasthenia Gravis

— PREVAIL trial found rapid improvement with a once-weekly subcutaneous injection

Results from the phase III PREVAIL trial presented at the American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine annual meeting showed that treatment with the investigational once-weekly nanobody gefurulimab significantly improved symptoms in adults with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, with a safety profile generally comparable to placebo.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, James Winkley, MD, of Baptist Health Medical Group in Lexington, Kentucky, discusses the findings, including the potential convenience of self-administered treatment with the subcutaneous injectable and compatibility with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy.

Following is a transcript of his remarks:

The PREVAIL study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with gefurulimab as the treating agent. Gefurulimab is a unique agent in that it's the first nanobody that'll be used in myasthenia gravis, which makes it a smaller molecule, which allows for greater tissue penetration and solubility -- so it can be given as a [subcutaneous] injection rather than the larger monoclonal antibodies, which have to be given in larger volumes underneath the skin or as IV infusion. So this would represent a greater ease of access for patients to have a [subcutaneous], once-a-week injection that doesn't require them to go to the infusion center.

As we had seen in the trial, similar to eculizumab [Bkemv] and ravulizumab [Ultomiris], which are C5 inhibitors, it met its primary outcome of MG-ADL [Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living] reduction, with a minus 4.2 reduction versus 2.1 on placebo, which was statistically significant. We did see a quick onset of action within 1 week, with a statistically significant reduction in the MG-ADL for those patients, as well as 4 weeks for the [Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis].

There were similar side effects between the treatment group and the placebo group, with injection-site reactions being slightly higher in the treatment group, but all of those reactions tended to be mild to moderate. The most common adverse events were headaches, upper respiratory infections, and muscle aches and pains. One thing that was significant at any time we're using complement inhibitors, there were no meningococcal infections. Everybody made sure they were fully vaccinated, and if they'd had to be started prior to 2 weeks, they received antibiotics. But we had a very typical safety profile, as I said, between the placebo arm and the treatment arm -- the side effects were similar.

This is going to make for ease of access for patients. You still have other molecules out on the market. You've got a once-daily complement inhibitor and you've got now a once-every-2-weeks IV infusion versus every 8 weeks. So kind of depending on what the patient prefers, this gives them greater access. We've got an easily portable complement inhibitor that patients no longer are tethered to an infusion center that they have to worry about. When's our next infusion? Do I have access? And I think that's going to be a huge advantage for the patients and their quality of life.

I would say that one thing that's unique about [gefurulimab] is that it is compatible with IVIG. And so the other larger monoclonal antibodies like the FcRn [neonatal Fc receptor] and the larger eculizumab and ravulizumab, it gets recycled by a different mechanism because it goes through the albumin on the FcRn receptor. It was combined with IVIG during the trial, patients could be on stable dosages of it, so it has that advantage of being able to be compared and not have to give supplemental dosing.

So I think that it will have combination with other available medications. I think that's a big advantage for it.

#5727. West Yorkshire’s £229 Million Bus Decisions Will Outlast Its Operating Contracts

West Yorkshire has made two substantial commitments to its bus network. On November 2, FirstGroup announced a £109 million agreement with the West Yorkshire Combined Authority covering five depots, associated infrastructure and 330 buses, including 79 battery-electric vehicles. The authority is also spending £120 million on more than 250 new buses through a separate programme. These investments will help establish the region’s new franchised Weaver Network, but many of the assets being acquired will remain in use long after the first operating contracts have ended.

West Yorkshire’s fleet and depot commitments illustrate a problem explored in my 83-page report, The Bus Is Not the System. The accompanying TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines which decisions are becoming expensive to reverse and what authorities should establish before making their next commitments.

The Weaver Network changes the relationship between public transport planning and private bus operations. The Combined Authority will specify services and retain responsibility for passenger revenue under its initial large contracts, while private operators deliver the routes. The region is securing assets that will remain important regardless of which company operates the buses. In principle, that can make future competition easier because bidders do not each have to provide a new depot and fleet.

The challenge is that buses, operating contracts and infrastructure follow different clocks. An operating contract might last five or seven years. Vehicles can work through successive contracts, while depot buildings and electrical connections may remain useful for decades. A change in route patterns, population or employment locations can make an established depot less convenient. A bus can often be reassigned, but a multi-megawatt electricity connection cannot be transferred to another site because the network needs charging capacity elsewhere.

West Yorkshire has arranged a staged transition. The five depot sales have completed, while the buses are scheduled to transfer as new franchises begin operating between May 2027 and October 2028. First Bus will continue delivering existing services under temporary depot leases and will manage electrification at Bradford and Huddersfield, with the authority paying for that work. The arrangements allow services and infrastructure development to proceed while ownership and operating responsibilities change.

Securing strategically important depots is a defensible approach. It reduces dependence on an incumbent operator’s control of scarce infrastructure and can help new companies compete for future contracts. The authority also assumes long-term responsibilities for the assets, including maintenance, future electrical capacity and their suitability for a changing passenger network. A depot can be worth purchasing without every potential alternative having been examined, but the consequences of losing those alternatives should be understood before the agreement becomes binding.

Electrification makes this especially important. Charging equipment, substations and electricity connections involve different suppliers, construction schedules and contractual responsibilities from the buses themselves. Vehicle orders can proceed before chargers are fully commissioned when the infrastructure delivery pathway is sufficiently assured. Problems arise when a fleet commitment depends on electrical capacity that cannot be delivered in time, or when the fallback arrangements are inadequate.

The passenger network can also change in ways that alter the original investment case. Better bus priority can reduce the number of vehicles needed to maintain a timetable. New housing developments can shift demand toward different corridors. A major employment centre or hospital relocation can change the value of existing routes and depots. The infrastructure secured today should support those possibilities rather than make sensible network improvements prohibitively expensive.

None of this argues for delaying every investment until uncertainty disappears. Authorities need to secure land, procure vehicles and obtain electrical connections years before some services begin. The useful distinction is between preparation that reduces uncertainty and commitments that substantially increase the cost of changing direction. Both need to be assessed against the passenger services the authority intends to deliver.

West Yorkshire’s programme offers a concrete example of the opportunity and challenge. Securing assets and specifying passenger services across the metropolitan network may produce a more coherent system than leaving every operator to optimize its own routes and depots. The long-term measure of success will be whether the authority can continue improving that network through changing demand, successive contracts and further electrification without having to reconstruct infrastructure it has already paid to provide.

This assessment concludes my five-part series drawn from The Bus Is Not the System, an 83-page TFIE Strategy report examining four decades of British and Irish metropolitan bus governance. The full West Yorkshire Briefing connects the report’s findings to current fleet, depot, electricity infrastructure and franchising decisions.

#5726. 1961 Chevy Impala Bubble Top For Sale With 1,111 Miles Shown Is A Wild LS V8 Restomod

When GM styling head Bill Mitchell set about redesigning the Chevrolet look for the 1961 model year, taking over from the iconic Harley Earl, he wanted to make a big shift away from the upright aesthetic with dramatic tail fins that defined the brand's 1950s. Moving into a smoother and cleaner jet age look, the 1961 Impala looked lower, longer, wider, and more streamlined. With wire-thin pillars and wraparound windows front and rear, the unique Sport Coupe model came to be known as a "bubbletop" in enthusiast circles. Decades on from its production date, this Impala design looks as beautiful as the day it was born. This particular example, currently for sale with a bubble-bursting $259,900 price tag, hides some modern improvements to make it an even better Impala.

Many car fanatics drive vintage cars because they're stylistically impressive, and it doesn't get much more impressive than a bubble top Impala scraping the ground on bags. There are downsides to driving a classic every day, though. Old cars typically don't have the modern amenities that American drivers have come to expect, like the unstoppable power of a fuel-injected small-block Chevrolet V8, a modern overdrive transmission, the stopping power of disc brakes, or modern air suspension. Thankfully, this Impala is fitted with all of these. This is a showstopper that was built to handle the rigors of modern traffic. What more could you want?

Take one part old Impala, one part modern Corvette, and one part creative hot-rod ingenuity, and you get a magnificent piece of automotive art. Albeit automotive art with the price tag of a long-lost Gertrude Abercrombie surrealist masterpiece. I want to know everything there is to know about this machine, and I bet you do, too.

While the car still carries all of the beautiful bodywork of a '61 Impala, it appears that just about everything under the skin has been replaced with modern alternatives. With new drivetrain components, suspension, steering, and brakes, this looks like a truly incredible driving experience waiting to happen. With the seller claiming just 1,111 miles on the odometer, it's just barely been broken in and should be taken on a nice long road trip with expediency. Imagine next summer cruising back and forth across the country on Route 66 in a black-over-red Impala and barely breaking a sweat because you have a nice fuel-efficient LS engine, graceful power steering, comfortable suspension, and ice-cold Vintage Air A/C blowing. Yeah, that's the American dream.

Back in 1961, Impala buyers would have been given three different engines to choose from, including a Blue Flame six-cylinder, a 283ci V8, and a 348ci V8. The most powerful Impala of its day featured 350 horsepower from a "Special Super Turbo-Thrust" V8 with three two-barrel carburetors. A modern LS2, cribbed from a C6 Corvette, makes an uncomplicated 400 ponies from its six-liter displacement. Presumably for the sake of simplicity and availability, the shop decided to pair this engine with a 4L60 four-speed automatic. This was an extremely common transmission, used in practically every rear-wheel drive General Motors product built from the mid-1990s to about 2010. This car should have no trouble delivering the giddyup, or laying some rubber if you want it to.

The seller describes the suspension setup thusly:

Equipped with a complete Ridetech Air Ride Suspension System, this Impala can transform from a pavement-hugging showpiece to a comfortable highway cruiser at the touch of a button!

Inside the Impala, there's an interesting juxtaposition of old and new, with gorgeous period-correct red interior upholstery wrapped around custom bucket seats, a unique center console, and plenty of retro-modern touches, like the full Dakota Digital gauge cluster. In addition to the modern air conditioning, this car is fitted with a modern (unspecified) multi-speaker sound system. I'm not sure how much music you'll need, considering the LS2's soundtrack is bolstered with a stainless-steel Borla exhaust.

I don't like the Billet Specialties wheels, and I think they're much too large for this car, but a nice set of 18s wouldn't go amiss here. Likewise, the steering wheel is a touch too far. Beyond that, I'm not sure there is much I would amend here. It's a nice car that appears to be nicely done. I'd want a few thousand more miles of testing on a completely custom car before taking it on a big trip, but the parts to fix it will be available at whatever parts counter you find along Route 66.

I'm not going to try to justify the price tag, because this is an absolutely absurd number, and I don't think they'll get anyone to pay it. If you have the spare quarter mil, though, there are a lot worse cars you could buy. Anything new in that price range is going to be faster, but will it be as effortlessly stylish? What's the point in buying a new Porsche 911 GT3 when a sea of them parks at your local cars and coffee? You could instead arrive in something that has show-worthy style, and you'd still have enough comfort to cross the country.

#5725. Another Drug Shows Potential for Functional Cures in Chronic Hepatitis B

— With highest dose of siRNA therapy, 19% achieved a functional cure 24 weeks after treatment ended

Reductions in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) were observed with a novel small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, according to a phase II study.

Among patients randomized to monotherapy with one of four doses of the siRNA HRS-5635, all 32 on the highest dose (400 mg) had HBsAg levels less than 100 IU/mL after 48 weeks of treatment, with 88% still at that level 24 weeks after treatment ended.

Among this high-dose group, 16% achieved a functional cure, with an HBsAg clearance level of less than 0.05 IU/mL after 48 weeks -- a percentage that rose to 19% by 24 weeks post-treatment, reported Xieer Liang, PhD, of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou, China, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

"A dose-dependent antiviral response was observed with HRS-5635," Liang said. "All HRS-5635 regimens were generally safe and well-tolerated."

An estimated 240 million people worldwide have chronic HBV infection, including about 640,000 U.S. adults. Chronic HBV can cause liver damage, cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death. Five antivirals and two immune modulators are approved in the U.S. to treat chronic HBV, with treatment regimens lasting from 6 months to over 1 year.

In a previous phase II trial, siRNA therapy with an immunomodulator reduced HBsAg in patients with chronic HBV infection. Last month, the FDA approved another nucleic acid-based therapeutic, the antisense oligonucleotide drug bepirovirsen (Hibsago), for patients with chronic HBV taking antiviral therapy based on results from the B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 studies. In those trials, 19% to 20% of patients with HBsAg levels between 100 and 3,000 IU/mL had a functional cure with bepirovirsen at week 72.

The current trial included patients with chronic HBV on stable nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy who had HBsAg levels over 100 and less than 3,000 IU/mL and HBV DNA levels less than 20 IU/mL. Patients could be hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) positive or negative, but they couldn't have cirrhosis. All patients received tenofovir amibufenamide during 48 weeks of HRS-5635 treatment.

Mean age ranged from 41.5 to 44.6 years in the four treatment groups, 59.4% to 76.7% were men, and mean HBsAg ranged from 1,058.2 IU/mL to 1,200.4 IU/mL. Most patients were HBeAg negative (65.6% to 73.3%).

The investigators defined functional cure as sustained HBV DNA suppression and HBsAg clearance of less than 0.05 IU/mL, with or without seroconversion, sustained for 24 weeks after treatment.

All four HRS-5635 doses achieved the study's primary endpoint of HBsAg reduction from baseline to week 12, with mean reductions of -1.26 log10 IU/mL in the 50-mg group, -1.90 log10 IU/mL in the 100-mg group, -1.99 log10 IU/mL in the 200-mg group, and -2.12 log10 IU/mL in the 400-mg group.

Among patients in the 400-mg group, 45% converted from HBeAg positive to HBeAg negative after 48 weeks of treatment, a percentage that slid to 27% at 24 weeks after treatment.

In patients receiving the 400-mg dose who were HBeAg negative and had HBsAg below 1,000 IU/mL at baseline, 33% reached the functional cure rate of HBsAg less than 0.05 IU/mL.

Across the four groups, 46.9% to 60% had a treatment-related adverse event. There were only two such events that were grade 3 or higher, and no serious adverse events related to treatment and no deaths occurred. Upper respiratory tract infections were the most common adverse event, occurring in 25% to 33.3% of patients in the four groups.

Alanine transaminase elevations occurred in up to 6.7% of patients during and after treatment, Liang said, but levels were generally stable during treatment, and no elevations reached a grade 3 level.

The follow-up period of 24 weeks after treatment ended was relatively short, Liang cautioned, but a longer-duration extension study is ongoing, along with a phase III trial.

#5722. Experience The Gales Of November With This Real-Time Great Lakes Simulator

#5721. RFK Jr. Is Ushering in Peptides. As an Oncologist, Here Are My Concerns.

— Clinical evidence hasn't caught up with commercial enthusiasm

On July 13, 2025, at a Las Vegas hotel hosting the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, two women were taken away in ambulances. Both had received injections containing experimental peptides at a conference booth. Both became seriously ill and required ventilators. One mixture was believed to contain MOTS-c, P21, BPC-157, and TB4, substances promoted for tissue repair, metabolic health, and longevity.

Both women recovered. Nevada regulators subsequently imposed $35,000 in fines on four parties involved. But investigators could not establish what caused the reactions. They were unable to obtain the injected products for laboratory testing, and their exact contents remain unverified.

That is what bothers me most: two women experienced life-threatening reactions, and investigators could not determine precisely what they received.

Now, Washington is opening a regulatory path for some of these unproven peptides. On October 28, HHS announced an interim enforcement-discretion policy covering six peptides: BPC-157, MOTS-c, TB-500, KPV, Semax, and Epitalon. Under specified conditions, the government does not intend to take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding these substances while the FDA considers formal rulemaking.

This is not an FDA approval, and it does not establish safety or effectiveness. While the HHS policy includes safeguards that represent progress, the policy also permits wider access before clinical evidence has caught up with commercial enthusiasm.

The question is not whether peptides have therapeutic potential. Many of them do. The question is whether that potential justifies their use before we know whether they work and are safe. The policy followed a July meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, which voted eight to six with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the compounding list. It also endorsed five of the other six substances considered.

FDA reviewers had reached a different conclusion. Their briefing documents found insufficient evidence to support adding any of the seven substances. For BPC-157, evaluated for ulcerative colitis, they could not establish effectiveness. For several others, including TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, and Epitalon, human safety studies were absent or extremely limited. Reviewers also identified problems with product characterization.

I have spent much of my career conducting oncology trials, including studies contributing to immunotherapies and targeted agents that are now used worldwide. I have seen promising mechanisms fail to translate into patient benefit and unexpected toxicities emerge after treatments entered routine practice. Clinical development is slow, expensive, and often disappointing. But it is how we distinguish a promising hypothesis from a useful medicine. We should make the review process more efficient, not bypass it.

I see a particular oncologic concern with the premature movement on peptides. Experimental studies suggest BPC-157 may stimulate angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, through pathways involving VEGFR2 and endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Angiogenesis supports normal tissue repair. It is also a process many tumors exploit to sustain growth. This does not mean BPC-157 causes cancer or promotes tumor progression -- we lack human evidence to make that claim. But neither can we definitively exclude such effects, particularly with prolonged exposure or in patients with existing or previously treated malignancies.

In oncology, we routinely encounter treatments acting on pathways shared by normal and malignant tissues. Biological activity beneficial in one setting may have unintended consequences in another. The response should not be to assume harm, but to investigate it.

There is also an indication mismatch. The FDA evaluated BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis, while much commercial interest concerns tendon injuries, exercise recovery, and anti-aging. Evidence for one indication cannot establish safety or effectiveness for another, particularly when doses, routes, and duration differ.

The HHS policy includes safeguards worth acknowledging: appropriately sourced ingredients, documentation of identity and purity, single-ingredient preparations, labeling, serious adverse-event reporting, and patient-specific prescriptions. These address genuine problems in the existing peptide market. Patients already obtain experimental substances through poorly regulated online suppliers. Licensed compounding under defined conditions could reduce some risks.

But we must distinguish between three questions:

Manufacturing controls help answer the first one. Toxicology and clinical studies address the second. Well-designed trials establish the third. A certificate of analysis cannot demonstrate effectiveness. A prescription does not establish a favorable benefit-risk ratio. Adverse-event reporting cannot replace prospective safety studies.

Compounding serves an important clinical purpose, meeting individual needs when commercial formulations are unsuitable. But it should not replace drug development. When experimental peptides are marketed through wellness clinics, telehealth, and social media to thousands of patients for similar purposes, they begin to resemble commercial drugs, even when prescriptions are individualized.

The same principle applies to longevity medicine. Research into cellular senescence, mTOR signaling, metabolic regulation, and cellular reprogramming offers genuine opportunities. I welcome it. But results in mice do not establish human benefit, and widespread use without systematic study does not necessarily generate reliable knowledge. We should accelerate research, not replace it with uncontrolled experimentation.

The HHS policy remains interim, with public comments invited through November 13. That process should address dosing, clinical benefit, long-term safety, adverse-event surveillance, and opportunities to link expanded access to systematic evidence generation.

The choice is not between innovation and regulation. Good regulation enables innovation while protecting patients from uncertain benefits and risks. We have learned this repeatedly in cancer drug development: a compelling mechanism begins a research program. It does not prove a drug is effective.

Innovation deserves encouragement. And patients deserve evidence.

#5720. At $14,000, Is This 1993 Toyota MR2 A Red-Hot Deal?

According to its seller, today's Nice Price or No Dice MR2 is a highly optioned model and was once sold on Bring a Trailer. It's been demoted to a Facebook Marketplace ad, and it's up to us to decide whether its price matches that lower-tier venue.

Rumored federal rollover safety standards effectively killed off convertible production in the U.S. from 1976 to the early '80s. The convertibles that boldly remained on the market during this time were all older cars like the MGB and Mercedes-Benz SL.

It was that latter convertible, the two-seater Benz, that served as the role model for the 1977 Cadillac Seville Milan we looked at on Monday. A custom-bodied two-seater convertible, the Milan attempted to fill that obvious gap in North America's car lineup. Unfortunately, the car's odd proportions gave the impression that upon arrival, its occupants would be revealed to be a congress of clowns rather than a chic couple with wind-tousled hair. That factor, plus questions about the car's condition, made us all question the seller's set $8,000 asking price. In short order, that dropped in an 82% 'No Dice' loss.

When it comes to styling and proportions, it's safe to say that Toyota hit the mark with the second-generation MR2. Larger, more cohesive, and roomier, the SW20 edition traded the first MR2's odd mini-Ferrari Mondial look for one more reverent to the better-looking Ferrari 328 GTB. It still checked all the boxes that made the first generation popular: a mid-engine layout, pop-up headlamps, and an optional T-top roof. Where the second-generation car strayed from the first was in size (it's substantially larger in almost all dimensions), and in the breathing of its top-models as the earlier cars' supercharger was traded for a turbo. One other distinction of the SW20 (perhaps unfairly) is that its handling at the limit can bite unwary drivers on the butt.

This 1993 MR2 comes in the officially named Super Red, making it a perfect accompaniment to the Man of Steel's cape and booties. This is a non-turbo car, so horsepower is limited to 135 ponies from the 5S-FE DOHC four. Fortunately, that engine is mated to a five-speed manual to make the most of that output. Even better, the seller says a new clutch was installed 46k miles ago, and the timing belt and water pump were refreshed just 26,000 miles back. New motor mounts, pads and rotors, and T-top seals are additional milestones in the car's service history.

This MR2 looks the part of a well-cared-for car, too. According to the seller, it was bought in Florida and spent much of its life in the South before being brought to New Jersey in 2018. When the present owner made that move, the car had 118,000 miles on the clock. It now has 136,788 miles, which averages about 2,400 miles a year under the current owner's care.

Overall, the car looks to be in great condition. The paint still pops, set off against factory alloys that show no evidence of injury. The engine looks cramped under its cover, and the sweeping buttresses make maintenance even more of a back-breaker, but at least it all looks intact.

The cabin doesn't appear cramped at all and looks quite handsome in its black-and-biscuit color scheme, with swanky leather upholstery on the seating surfaces. It all appears stock in here, save for a TRD-branded leather shift knob, although that does keep it in the family.

On the downside, the seller warns that the A/C compressor is grinding and hence they've removed the belt to keep it from turning and potentially doing more damage. The ad also makes no mention of the tires' age or condition. With so few miles driven each year, it's easy to let tires hang on longer than they should. The MR2 features a staggered setup, with larger, wider wheels in the back, meaning that rotating front to rear is out of the question, making the meats even more out of sight, out of mind.

On the plus side, the ad notes that all of the car's glass has been VIN-etched as an anti-theft measure. In addition, the car comes with a clean title, not one but two options for T-top storage, and three keys. Oddly, though the seller says this was a heavily optioned car, it does not seem to have a remote-entry key fob. Weird. There are also two manila folders full of maintenance records going back to the previous owner. Those will accompany the car in the sale.

On the face of it, this appears to be a solid example of a stock, mostly complete second-gen non-turbo MR2 with all the right specs and the promise of a well-managed service history. What's not to like, right? Well, there's that sweaty-Betty non-working A/C. That's going to cost a pretty penny to fix. We should also probably consider a new set of tires unless, upon inspection, they still seem to be in the game. Other than that, there don't seem to be any major red flags on this car. Plus, who doesn't dig an old MR2?

That only leaves us with the car's $14,000 asking price to either rejoice or bemoan. Let's talk about that. What's your opinion on this MR2 at that $14,000 asking? Does that sound fair given the car's presentation and specs? Or, at that price, is this Mister a miss?

Facebook Marketplace out of Tenafly, New Jersey, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5719. Sierra Club Welcomes CalPERS’ $71 Billion Climate-Solutions Investment Milestone, Urges Fund to End Financing of Fossil Fuel Expansion

SACRAMENTO, CA — On Monday, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) reported that the value of investments it classifies as climate solutions reached $71 billion as of June 30, 2026, up from $59.7 billion a year earlier. The increase brings the nation’s largest public pension fund closer to its goal of $100 billion in climate investments by 2030.

Sierra Club welcomed CalPERS’ continued commitment to climate-solutions investing and called on the fund to adopt stronger standards and transparency around what counts toward its $100 billion goal. Sierra Club also urged CalPERS to prioritize investments that support real-world emissions reductions and address climate risks across its broader portfolio to protect the retirement security of the workers and retirees it serves.

In response, Ben Cushing, Director of Sierra Club’s Sustainable Finance Campaign, released the following statement:

“It’s encouraging to see CalPERS make progress toward its climate-solutions goal, but a growing investment total doesn’t tell us how much new money is helping build clean energy and cut emissions. Reducing climate risk also means looking at where CalPERS invests across the whole portfolio. CalPERS has already taken the important step of using its votes to hold company directors accountable for how they handle climate risk. It can build on that work by adopting a policy to stop financing fossil fuel expansion and backing climate projects that need new investment to get built or expand.”

CalPERS said the $11.3 billion increase came from both new investments and gains on assets it already held. CalPERS also reported that financed emissions across the asset classes covered by its analysis rose by approximately 6 percent over the past year, largely reflecting investments in higher-emitting assets that it expects to decarbonize over time. For its global public equity and U.S. corporate credit holdings, CalPERS reported an implied temperature rise of 2.9°C, up from 2.7°C a year earlier.

Last year, Sierra Club and the California Common Good coalition urged CalPERS to publish a full list of the investments it counts toward its $100 billion goal, adopt science-based standards for what qualifies as a climate solution, and exclude fossil fuel investments from that total. Sierra Club has raised these concerns at CalPERS board meetings, and elaborated on them in a December 2025 CalMatters op-ed questioning the credibility and real-world impact of CalPERS’ reported climate investments.

Sierra Club’s 2025 Principles for Climate Solutions Investments outline standards for credible investing, including prioritizing real-world emissions reductions and establishing safeguards for transition financing. Its January 2026 Climate Solutions Gap report likewise highlighted CalPERS as an example of why ambitious climate-solutions targets must be backed by credible definitions, clear eligibility criteria, and transparent reporting.

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. For more information, visit www.sierraclub.org.

#5718. What Car Looks Best On Aftermarket Wheels?

Let's face it: Most stock wheels are, at best, fine. Occasionally one will stand out for its looks, usually because it's been made by Mercedes, but most OEM wheels are just some basic metal that you can wrap a tire around. That's good enough for getting from point A to point B, but we car enthusiasts often want better. Enter the entire world of aftermarket wheels, in any style you could dream up — rally turbofans, classic five-spokes, even teddy bears.

Today, though, we're not here to talk about the wheels themselves. We're here to talk about the cars they go on, and that brings us to a very broad question: What car looks best on aftermarket wheels? I'll accept answers to this in two forms, either cars that most need aftermarket wheels or cars that look best on the most different designs of aftermarket wheel. Are those criteria wide-open enough for you?

For both versions of the question, I think there's a single answer: The Toyobaru, most specifically the first-generation Scion FR-S/Subaru BRZ. It's a car that looks great on lightweight track wheels like Volk TE37s or Titan 7 T-S5s, but its style is just as well-suited to a set of bags and a BBS mesh design. Even a vintage wheel like the RS Watanabe, when scaled up to modern fitment, looks great on the Toyobaru chassis.

I think the car that looks best on aftermarket wheels is the first-generation Scion FR-S/Subaru BRZ, but what do you think? Do you think the Civic most needs a new set of shoes, or that the Lexus LS400 can do no wrong with any style of wheel face? Let me know in the comments below, and I'll collect my favorite answers later in the week. Bonus points if you've tried aftermarket wheels on a chassis yourself.

#5717. New BYD Seal 07 Illustrates Chinese EV Evolution

Last week, BYD introduced the next generation Seal 07 EV. This model replaces the original BYD Seal, which entered the market in late 2022 and put the brand on the map in the minds of many people around the world. While the new vehicle is important to BYD, it also illustrates many of the changes that have happened to the EVs and the EV market in China over the past few years.

The new Seal 07 grows to 5080 mm long by 1960 mm wide by 1495 mm tall. That compares to 4,800 mm long, 1,875 mm wide and 1,460 mm high for the previous Seal. That also makes it slightly larger than the late Tesla Model S.

Like many new BYD cars, the interior has become more premium and technologically advanced.  Interiors offer front zero gravity seats with heating, ventilation and massage. An onboard refrigerator is offered in the center console and a power sunshade in the roof. Speakers have proliferated. The screens have improved,  programmable buttons can be added, and voice interaction has improved. Basic versions come with BYD’s God’s Eye C with BYD covering autonomous parking, while higher trims offer LiDAR-based God’s Eye B with BYD adding coverage for city navigation.

Seal 07 models now come with DiSus-C adaptive damping on lower trim models and DiSus-M magnetorheological active dampers on higher trims. Suspension is double wishbones up front, multilink at the rear.

Of course, the new car offers BYD’s flash charging, capable of charging from 10-70% in 5 minutes and 10-97% in 9 minutes, while taking 12 minutes to go from 10-97% at -30 C with no preconditioning. 20,000 BYD flash charging stations are planned to be in operation by the end of the year, which will be more than all DC charging stations in the US combined. Meanwhile, the previous Seal took 26 minutes to go from 30-80%.

Looking at the closest version of the original Seal from 2022, battery capacity has dropped from 82.5 kW to 76.4 kW for the new model. Meanwhile, range increased to 775 km CLTC from 700 km in the old model due to greater efficiency. While efficiency may have once been a criticism of the Seal, it is now a highlight. Power is up from 230 kW to 245 kW (329 hp). Meanwhile, a curb weight of 1975 kg is lighter than the previous 700 km model (2055 kg), with increased use of UHSS in the structure.

Overall, it is a larger and more luxurious car than the vehicle it replaces, while losing a little weight. Performance, charging and efficiency have improved. Equipment levels are higher. Technology is more advanced. And then we get to affordability.

In 2022, the original Seal offered a 550 km range trim for 209,800 RMB ($31,424 USD at current exchange rates), but the 700 km range version, which is closest to the new model, started at 259,800 RMB ($38,913).

A little over 4 years later, the new Seal 07 EV starts at 149,900 RMB ($22,437 USD) with 775 km of range, more power and much faster charging. It costs 10,000 RMB ($1498) more for a version with God’s Eye C intelligent driving. For the top-of-the-line flagship with LiDAR-based God’s Eye B, the price is 184,900 RMB ($27,694 USD). In addition, there are launch discounts and perks. Of note, there is no AWD version of the new Seal 07, with that role filled by other BYD models in China.

For the default comparison, the standard RWD Model 3 is smaller (4720 mm long) slower, comes with less equipment and only 634 km of CLTC range (612 km with optional 19” wheels). Price starts at 225,500 RMB, although paint colors and interior options increase the price (included with the Seal). To get Enhanced Driver Assistance, which is roughly equivalent to God’s Eye C, you need to add on 32,000 RMB, while Tesla Driver Assist (similar to God’s Eye B) adds on 64,000 RMB ($9,586 USD). To get as close to a top spec Seal 07 in a standard Model 3, would take you to 307,500 ($46,057), but you would still be under-equipped with less range in a smaller, less powerful vehicle. The Long Range RWD would take you to a bit above the Seal 07 with 800 km of range on 19” wheels, even though that ternary  battery is recommended not to charge to 100% on a regular basis, unlike the LFP-based second generation Blade Battery in the BYD. The Long Range RWD Model 3 costs 331,500 RMB ($49,652 USD) with paint, 19” wheels and Driver Assist, but still lacks in equipment.

However, the Seal 06 (4870 mm) is a better match for the standard Model 3 but comes in at 119,900 to 159,900 RMB ($17,958 to $23,950 USD). There is also a no-compromise, larger (5150 mm) Seal 08 with more available range, power and amenities from 196,900 to 239,900 RMB ($29,492-$35,932 USD). And if you want something sportier, there is now the Fang Cheng Bao Formula S (5060 mm) at 189,900 to 229,900 RMB ($28,443-$34,434 USD). For something more luxurious, there is the Denza Z9S at 255,800 to 325,800 RMB ($38,313-$48,798 USD). None of those BYD models existed when the original Seal was launched. In addition, there are also Dynasty Han and Qin sedans from BYD for a little different flavor. And those are just the BEV models. There are also PHEV versions.

Looking beyond Tesla and BYD, the Seal 07 fits in the price gap between the Mona M03 and Next P7 at XPENG. It slots below the SU7 from Xiaomi. Below a Zeekr 7X or Nio ET5. At its current price, size and capability, the Seal 07 is in a good competitive niche between entry level sedans and more premium vehicles. If the Seal 07 had kept the original Seal’s higher price point, the competition would be much more challenging.

Compared to 2022, the new Seal 07 does not need to cover as many bases. This lets it better meet the needs of specific customers, while related models can be tailored to different customer needs. Undoubtedly, these different models will divide sales numbers, which may not be good for bragging rights. Analysis will become more challenging and may require combining sales of related models for relevant comparisons. But the increased choice is better for customers.

It may be a while before we have a clear picture of what impact this all has on sales. Chinese regulations that began earlier this year prevent manufacturers or dealers from selling below cost. This essentially prohibits the model-year-end clearance sales that are typical throughout much of the West. In addition, Chinese regulations stopped the practice of registering a vehicle and then exporting it as a zero-mile used car. In combination, it becomes much more difficult to manage inventory. As such, many models that are about to be replaced have their deliveries cut well in advance of the new model launch and have sales essentially evaporate. Then, it can take a while for the new models to ramp up production and deliveries to take hold. We may not have a good picture of BYD’s sedan sales in China until next year.

It also may be a while before we have global distribution plans or pricing for the new models. The three new Seal models are not yet offered outside of China. BYD has taken the approach of waiting to bring their latest models to export markets, often introducing models overseas as new that have already been discontinued in China. When they do offer current models, they tend to be at a significant premium (see Denza Z9GT). Meanwhile, companies like XPENG are introducing their latest models globally.

However, with intensifying competition from Chinese automakers in some export markets, BYD’s approach may change. Some flash charging cars are starting to reach export markets. The Seagull (ATTO 1) has recently been selling in Australia for $19,990 AUD ($13,752 USD), representing a significant reduction in export markup. We might see more advanced models at lower markups in markets where protectionism has not taken hold.

For comparison to the US, the least expensive car of any powertrain is the gasoline Kia K4 at $23,535, which is more than the base Seal 07 ($22,437). The least expensive EV is the soon-to-be-discontinued Chevy Bolt at $28,995, which is more than the most expensive Seal 07 ($27,694). Meanwhile, the least expensive EV sedan in the US is once again the Tesla Model 3 at $38,630 (including destination and fees, which are included in Chinese prices). A number of other EV models were canceled.

In China, EV choices have expanded, cars have become more capable, and prices have come down over the past four years. Meanwhile, in the US, cars remain unaffordable and EV choices have diminished with aging products.

Of note, the original BYD Seal had already attained regulatory approval from Transport Canada for import prior to Biden and Trudeau implementing prohibitive 100%+ tariffs on Chinese cars. Due to regulatory harmonization between the two countries, that meant it would have also been approved to enter the US. The US EV market could have looked dramatically different now, even with the rollback of consumer subsidies. With free trade, we could be looking at an EV growth in market share, expansion of options and improvement in affordability similar to China, even if not to the same extent.

Overall, the new Seal 07 is a strong entrant into a competitive segment in a very competitive market. It might be a challenge to choose it over one of the many other excellent options from BYD and its competitors in China. However, having too many excellent, affordable EV options to choose from is a good challenge for customers to have.

#5716. Honda Goes All-In On Hybrids With New $3 Billion Plant In Ohio

Good morning! It's Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Honda is spending billions on a new hybrid vehicle plant in Ohio, Waymos still love blasting past stopped school buses, Stellantis angers a Canadian auto workers union by officially selling its Brampton assembly plant to a defense contractor, and NHTSA is probing 1.2 million Fords because their side airbags are allegedly burning passengers when they're deployed.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Honda's EV plans flopped hard and cost the Japanese automaker big time. Now, it's pivoting to hybrids in a huge way, and a large part of that is a brand new $3 billion factory in central Ohio that is meant to boost capacity for its most popular vehicles. The new plant is slated to start cranking out vehicles in 2029, expanding its output by 240,000 vehicles per year.

The move is an inflection point for Honda — part of a strategic pivot that started earlier this year when it threw in the towel on electric vehicles in America. The write-down on that decision cost the company $15.7 billion and caused its first annual loss since going public in 1957. Now, it aims to introduce 15 new hybrids globally by March of 2030, with North America as the primary target. From Bloomberg:

The new facility will be located between two existing auto assembly plants it operates in Ohio. It will be tooled to build gas-only, hybrid and fully electric vehicles, but the company didn't provide a breakdown by production volume.

Honda also wouldn't say which vehicles will be made in the new plant, but its focus will be on boosting output of models offering a hybrid option, including all-new models.

In a separate statement, it announced an investment of C$166 million ($118 million) in its Canadian factory in Alliston, Ontario, to make next-generation vehicles and for "the reintroduction of engine manufacturing."

Honda was prepared to spend C$15 billion on an EV battery supply chain complex in Canada, but put that plan on indefinite hold in May. It also canceled a trio of battery-electric models it was preparing to manufacture in the US. But it began production this summer of battery cells at a $4.4 billion joint venture with LG Energy Solution in Ohio.

That facility was originally designed to build batteries for electric vehicles but has pivoted to make hybrid batteries, [Honda U.S. executive vice president Bob] Nelson said.

Honda has vehicle assembly operations in Ohio, Alabama and Indiana as well as in Canada and Mexico. In addition, it makes key parts such as engines and transmissions in Alabama, Georgia and Ohio. The company said on Monday that it will also make investments in a number of other facilities in North America, but not at its Mexican plant.

Despite the doom and gloom of this year's overall financials, the automaker itself is having a fairly solid year. Honda's U.S. sales have actually risen 5% in the first 10 months of 2026, thanks to strong demand for hybrid versions of the CR-V, Accord, and Civic. Clearly, Honda is following the money, and right now the money is in hybrids. As it stands, hybrids make up about a third of the company's total sales volume in the U.S., and that's while the lineup is missing hybrids in key players like the Pilot and Passport — not to mention, the entire Acura brand.

Last year, I visited Japan and got a look at Honda's next-generation V6 hybrid powertrain, which is meant for larger vehicles. Don't be shocked if it ends up in the MDX and aforementioned Pilot sooner rather than later. There's also news that Acura is working on a Passport-based off-road eight-passenger hybrid SUV, and that's sure to be something rather neat.

The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it had opened a recall inquiry into Alphabet's Waymo because the damn things keep passing stopped school buses. You and I, people who passed driver's ed, know you're not supposed to do that. But these robogoofuses somehow can't get that through their thick, electronic skulls. I mean, it's something we've reported on numerous times before.

The probe will look into nearly 3,000 Waymos with the goal of determining whether a software update that Waymo rolled out last year failed to stop the robotaxis from passing stopped school buses with flashing red lights. Odds are that it didn't, as most of the violations allegedly happened after the company said the remedy had been deployed. Oopsy. From Reuters:

In October 2025, NHTSA opened a preliminary evaluation into the issue of ​Waymo vehicles illegally passing stopped school buses. The agency closed that investigation on Monday ​in favor of the new recall query to determine the cause of the additional violations.

In Austin, Texas, the independent school district documented 19 distinct violations and issued numerous $300 tickets to ​Waymo. Six other violations were recorded by public schools in Atlanta.

NHTSA said it ​was reviewing the software update implemented by Waymo under a December 2025 recall. The auto safety regulator said ‌most ⁠of the incidents occurred after November 2025, when Waymo said it had completed the software remedy for all affected vehicles.

NHTSA's query is meant to assess how well Waymo's remedy actually worked and then determine the causes of the post-remedy incidents. Just to add to all the fun, the NTSB is also investigating.

The long saga is finally over. Stellantis seems to have a deal to sell its Brampton Assembly plant in Canada to none other than armored-car maker Roshel. The transaction, if it closes at the end of the year, would bring an end to vehicle manufacturing at the Ontario factory, which has been a flashpoint in the U.S.-Canada trade war. It's also likely to trigger all sorts of labor tensions among the company's unionized employees. Unifor said Stellantis' Brampton plans prompted an impasse in talks on a new labor deal, and they called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to block the sale. From The Wall Street Journal:

Stellantis' turnaround plan laid out earlier this year calls for using a higher share of its North American factory space by 2030. The automaker has too much factory space relative to its North American sales, said Sam Fiorani, vice president of consulting firm AutoForecast Solutions. "Taking Brampton offline removes some idle capacity," Fiorani said.

The Brampton factory was built four decades ago, and has floor space of nearly three million square feet, or about five football fields.

Roman Shimonov, the founder and CEO of Roshel, said he wants to build a top-tier manufacturing operation in Brampton, adding the transaction promises to drive job creation in Canadian manufacturing. Shimonov had previously said that Roshel was ready to bring affected Stellantis workers on board as part of the new production facility.

Unifor, unsurprisingly, is not thrilled with the news.

The reassurances didn't sit well with Lana Payne, president of Unifor. She said Stellantis "betrayed" the company's 9,000 unionized workers "with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments."

Stellantis said in September it was contemplating a sale of the Brampton factory to Roshel, as a return to auto production was deemed financially unfeasible.

The Brampton plant has remained idle since 2024 due to retooling, and Stellantis had plans to manufacture the next-generation Jeep Compass at the Canadian factory. Those plans changed after President Trump imposed hefty tariffs on foreign-made vehicles.

Instead, Stellantis said it would shift production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, citing trade and market conditions. That move angered Canadian officials, given that federal and regional governments provided over $700 million in taxpayer-backed financing to retool the Brampton factory, as well as a plant in Windsor, Ontario.

Canadian officials have, on several occasions, threatened to sue Stellantis to recoup the money.

In a statement, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said officials would focus on helping the 2,000 impacted workers in Brampton, and she urged the union, the automaker and regional authorities to meet this week to come up with some sort of a solution. However, her statement doesn't make any mention of pursuing legal action against the automaker.

Last month, Stellantis workers voted to formally give Unifor the mandate to pursue a strike in Canada amid stalled talks.

Federal safety regulators are probing 1.2 million 2021-2026 Ford Explorers after several drivers allegedly suffered burns after their side airbags deployed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says the investigation centers on complaints that the deployment of seat-mounted side airbags was causing serious burns. So far, it has received eight Vehicle Owner Questionnaires and four Early Warning Reporting "Death and Injury" reports related to the issue. From the Detroit Free Press:

"Consumers have described that during a crash involving deployment of the seat-mounted side airbag, they sustained burn injuries," NHTSA's report read. "Burn injuries have been reported for both drivers and front passengers and were typically diagnosed as second or third-degree burns requiring medical treatment."

The NHTSA document went on to say that some of the Vehicle Owner Questionnaires report injuries were to law enforcement officers following side airbag deployments in Ford Explorer Police Interceptors. According to a recent report by CNBC, more than half of the 12,000 U.S. police departments drive Ford vehicles. It said Ford claims it has two-thirds of the police market with the General Motors and Stellantis supplying the balance.

A spokesman for Ford Motor told the Detroit Free Press on Nov. 9 that the company might have a comment on NHTSA's announced preliminary evaluation later. Ford makes the Explorer at its Chicago Assembly Plant in Illinois.

I can't exactly say something like this is shocking. I mean, so far this year, Ford has issued 85 recalls, and second-place Stellantis is only at 41. It has literally lapped the field, and if this inquiry turns into a recall, it'll only add to that total.

#5715. Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Could Soon Get an Effective Therapy

— Drug already approved for dermatomyositis passes phase II test

ORLANDO -- Patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis -- a condition with no very effective therapy -- saw dramatic improvement with the dual-acting TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor brepocitinib (Lisraya) in a small phase II trial.

Patients treated with either of two doses of brepocitinib achieved 22-point reductions in Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Activity and Morphology Instrument-Activity (CSAMI-A) scores after 16 weeks, well above the 5-point threshold for clinical relevance, compared with no decrease at all with placebo, reported Misha Rosenbach, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

The drug also showed strong efficacy for secondary outcomes, the group found, and no serious adverse effects were recorded. The study was published in JAMA Dermatology and was also presented here at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis might be the biggest treatment challenge in all of dermatology. Corticosteroids have long been the mainstay of therapy, but are only sporadically effective and, among patients who do respond, relapses are common. Second-line treatments such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, or tetracyclines don't do much better. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were recommended as third-line therapy in a 2021 treatment guideline, but on very poor evidence. A French case series published in 2017 suggested TNF inhibitors could be used effectively, but the authors noted that adverse effects and discontinuations were common, and one-third of patients relapsed while on therapy.

With this dismal treatment landscape in mind, clinicians have turned to Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors as a possible alternative. Drugs such as tofacitinib (Xeljanz) and upadacitinib (Rinvoq) have been tried with some success, but only in single case reports and small series. Good results were also reported last year with the currently approved TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib (Sotyktu) in one patient.

All that bodes well for brepocitinib, which the FDA approved in August for dermatomyositis, and the phase II data in sarcoidosis appear to bear out the promise. Rosenbach and colleagues enrolled 31 patients, randomizing them in a 3:2:2 ratio to 45 or 15 mg/day of brepocitinib or placebo; they could stay on their conventional non-targeted therapies, but oral steroids were withdrawn over the first 8 weeks and topical steroids were stopped at randomization.

Patients were generally in their 40s and 50s. Mean disease duration varied in the three arms: about 10 years for the placebo and high-dose brepocitinib groups, and 4 years in the low-dose group. CSAMI-A scores averaged about 34 at baseline. Roughly 40% of participants had lupus pernio, the lumpy discolored facial and cranial lesions that may be the worst symptom of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Pulmonary sarcoidosis was also common in the sample.

Change from baseline in CSAMI-A score was the primary outcome measure. While no difference between the two brepocitinib doses was seen for this endpoint, "high-bar" outcomes showed some gaps. All patients in the high-dose group saw at least 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores, compared with 73% on the low dose (and 14% in the placebo group). Similarly, "functional remission," defined as a score below 5, was achieved by 62% with 45 mg versus 46% on 15 mg, and none receiving placebo.

Perhaps most encouragingly, all five patients in the 45-mg group with lupus pernio achieved 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores. Patients on the active drug also had substantial improvement in skin-related quality of life, whereas the placebo group actually had deterioration. (The near-total lack of improvement with placebo for any efficacy outcome testifies to just how difficult cutaneous sarcoidosis is to treat.)

With regard to safety, one patient in each arm quit therapy because of adverse events. But none were rated as serious. One patient on 45 mg showed a creatinine kinase elevation, and one developed anemia. Otherwise, no "special interest" events were seen; these included cardiovascular events, viral reactivation, transaminase elevations, venous thromboembolism, and malignancies.

Following his conference presentation, Rosenbach was asked where brepocitinib might fit in the treatment algorithm for cutaneous sarcoidosis. He cautioned that it was still early to speculate on that, since a larger phase III trial is only just getting underway. But if those data are like those he reported, "I imagine many patients would get it as first line," he said.

He was also asked about effects on pulmonary and joint manifestations, which are common in cutaneous sarcoidosis. He said the studies thus far have really focused on skin, and he couldn't say much about other symptoms. He added, though, that these would almost certainly be examined in the phase III trial.

Brepocitinib's developer, Priovant Therapeutics, expects primary results from the phase III study at the end of 2028. Rosenbach said the 45-mg dose will be the one tested for potential approval. Additional trials are underway in uveitis and lichen planopilaris; there's no indication, however, that Priovant plans to challenge deucravacitinib, which is approved for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.

#5713. 5 Years In, Mustang Mach-E Battery Data Shows What Real-World Electric Vehicle Durability Looks Like

Five years ago, the first Mustang Mach-E customers began adding something important to the Ford electric vehicle battery validation work: real-world ownership at scale.

As part of our quality process, design and validation engineering starts long before a vehicle reaches a customer. We model battery performance, run physical tests, expose packs to heat, cold, and charging profiles, and build in margin for demanding real-world conditions.

These rigorous quality tests are designed to help us understand how battery systems perform across a wide range of climates, charging behaviors, and driving conditions before customers get behind the wheel.

Then David Blenkle drove past 400,000 miles on the original battery in his 2022 Mustang Mach-E. He gave us a real-world example of what is possible — and begged the question of whether he’s an outlier or not.

His battery health has remained strong through unusually high-mileage use. His experience gave our team a chance to compare one exceptional ownership case with what we are seeing across the broader fleet.

The bigger question was if David’s experience reflected a broader pattern. So, we decided to look back at the Mustang Mach-E owners who started it all: The Class of 2021.

Over five years ago, the first Mustang Mach-E vehicles — model year 2021 — reached customers. Those electric SUVs have been on the road, in customers’ hands, ever since.

We analyzed the battery state-of-health data for the entire fleet.

Here is what the Class of 2021 looks like at the five-year mark:

More than 36,000 vehicles. Two billion all-electric miles, across all 50 states and across Canada.

Our Class of 2021 has almost reached Neptune — not a practical comparison, but a useful way to understand the scale and distance.

The number I look at closely is the spread. Ninety-five percent of those vehicles fall between 87% and 97% health. Averages can hide variation, so that range matters.

In some cases, David has driven 300,000 miles more than many in our 2021 cohort. Then there are also the people who are road-warriors, like David.

More than 2,000 Class of 2021 owners have crossed 100,000 miles on their original battery, averaging better than 91% battery health. A smaller group of high-mileage drivers — more than 30 drivers past 200,000 miles — is averaging 88%.1

David’s mileage remains exceptional, but the broader Class of 2021 data shows he is part of a larger pattern of strong battery health across real-world use.

Long-term battery health remains one of the biggest questions for many people considering an electric vehicle, and real-world data like this helps make that conversation more concrete.

Two billion customer-driven miles is meaningful because it reflects how people use their vehicles — commuting, road-tripping, and running their everyday lives.

And it’s not just the 2021 Mustang Mach-E.

Aggregated across the full battery-electric lineup released over the last five years in the U.S. and Canada, the pattern holds: our packs are designed to last at least 10 years, and in the wild they’re maintaining, on average, greater than 90% health at 100,000 miles.2

The Class of 2021 is the cohort old enough, right now, to tell the most detailed version of that story.

While this story focuses on the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, the learning doesn’t stop there.

Ford uses field data from vehicles on the road to inform current and future electric vehicle programs such as the Universal Electric Vehicle platform and Fathom. This includes how we think about battery management, charging guidance, and long-term ownership confidence.

Battery chemistry is complicated, but a few simple everyday habits can help support long-term battery health:

Owners should not have to become battery chemistry experts to take good care of their electric vehicles.

The 2021 Mustang Mach-E vehicles in this data set use NCM battery chemistry, where frequent full charges are generally not needed for daily use. Some newer Ford EV batteries use LFP chemistry, which benefits from an occasional charge to 100% to help the battery management system stay calibrated.

Ford over time has implemented new features, like guidance in the Ford App, to help owners look after their batteries, specific to the vehicle and battery system they drive.

I have spent my career on the battery side of this business — cell chemistry, pack design, thermal management, and the systems that help a battery perform over time.

For an owner, the battery is central to the EV experience. It shapes confidence in every commute, road trip, and charging stop.

This is one of the most valuable feedback loops we have had at this scale: more than 36,000 vehicles, five-plus years, and billions of real-world miles.

The data is encouraging, and the learnings continue to inform how Ford approaches battery systems, software guidance, and future electric vehicle programs.

The Class of 2021 has added a real-world chapter to what our validation work was designed to understand. And we have many more electric miles ahead of us.

By Kevin Vander Laan, the Technical Leader of High-Voltage Battery Cells and Systems at Ford.

1. Battery state-of-health data is as of August 2026 for all 21MY Mustang Mach-E vehicles sold to U.S. and Canada retail and fleet customers, covering approximately 36,000 owners with an average ownership period of 5.2 years. Figures reflect usable battery capacity.

2. Based on a 2026 manufacturer field data study of high-voltage battery state of health on Ford battery electric vehicles.

#5711. More than 300 Solar & Storage Companies Urge Congress to Pass Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Accelerate Clean Energy Deployment, Lower Costs

WASHINGTON D.C. — More than 300 solar and storage companies are urging Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), S. 5653, warning that outdated federal permitting processes and grid infrastructure bottlenecks are delaying critical energy projects and driving up electricity costs.

In a letter to congressional leaders, the companies call on lawmakers to quickly send the bipartisan legislation to the President’s desk. The signatories note that solar and storage account for 70% of new electricity capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026, while $120 billion in clean energy investment remains caught in permitting delays.

“You can’t lower energy costs if you can’t build the energy projects, and these companies know that this bipartisan legislation will help get America building again,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).

BAAJA would modernize the federal permitting system by ensuring fair treatment for all technologies, protecting lawfully issued permits from politically motivated delays, establishing predictable timelines for federal reviews and judicial proceedings, modernizing transmission planning, and expanding distributed energy resources’ access to wholesale electricity markets.

New SEIA analysis shows that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.

The message from more than 300 companies comes as voters made clear in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs is a top concern. Permitting reform is urgently needed to meet rising demand and get more reliable, affordable solar and storage projects built.

About SEIA®: The Solar Energy Industries Association® (SEIA) is leading the transformation to a clean energy economy. SEIA works with its 1,200 member companies and other strategic partners to fight for policies that create jobs in every community and shape fair market rules that promote competition and the growth of reliable, low-cost solar power. Founded in 1974, SEIA is the national trade association for the solar and solar + storage industries, building a comprehensive vision for the Solar+ Decade through research, education and advocacy. Visit SEIA online at www.seia.org and follow @SEIA on Twitter, LinkedIn, and Instagram.
