#5604. Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating

The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security.

At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer.

Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy.

Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May.

He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc.

Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country.

Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol.

Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice.

But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything, according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.”

Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing.

Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported.

Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it.

However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday, wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation.

Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.

#5603. Douglas Elliman Goes All-In for AI After Q3’s Flat Earnings

After a middling third quarter, Douglas Elliman CEO Michael Liebowitz told investors that recent changes and efforts to the company are to “modernize” and build a “more efficient platform” by early 2027.

The luxury brokerage’s revenue fell short in the third quarter at $252.1 million for 2026, a $10 million drop compared to 2025’s revenue of $262.8 million.

For the first nine months of the year, revenue also dropped and was reported at $749.9 million. In 2025, that revenue was reported at $787.6 million.

During the Q3 earnings call for Douglas Elliman, Liebowitz claimed that the last quarter was about “technological upgrades” and emphasized the company’s movement toward execution.

“Technology is central to our strategy, and the transformation we introduced last quarter has continued to advance as part of our broader efforts to modernize the business and reduce costs,” he stated.

The company has faced struggles both in the market and internally over the past two years, with C-suite turnover and competition in its home market of New York City.

After the earnings report, the company’s stock jumped 12%, though it is still down 30% this year.

Liebowitz also mentioned multiple additions to Douglas Elliman this past quarter, including Sharon Milz as head of AI technology transformation, Nick Patino as director of AI enablement and Jamie Gagliano as chief operations officer.

“Sharon is overseeing our enterprise AI strategy and deployment as well as the broader technology transformation across the company,” he added. “Nick focuses on making sure these capabilities become part of how we get things done across the company, translating new technology into adoption, productivity and measuring business value. Jamie brings significant experience working with agents and building businesses. She’s already looking across our national operations at how we simplify processes, strengthen support and build a more scalable organization.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Aside from a drop in revenue, Douglas Elliman also reported a drop in operating income (loss) annually. For Q3 2026, the company reported an operating income of $6.3 million, while last year’s operating loss clocked in at $10.7 million.

Bryant Kirkland—Douglas Elliman’s CFO—stated on the Q3 earnings call, however, that the year-over-year comparisons lean negatively because of 2025’s data.

“The year-over-year comparisons for the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026 are impacted by a difficult comparable, due to an unusually strong first quarter of 2025,” he noted.

Adjusted EBITDA—or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization—may signal positive growth for the brokerage, as Q3’s EBITDA was $5.3 million compared to last year’s $1 million.

While the adjusted EBITDA grew for Q3, the company’s adjusted net loss greatly overshadows many gains, as it reported the adjusted net loss at nearly $8 million, compared to last year’s $1.4 million.

Existing-home sales, Kirkland mentioned, were up 1.9% from October 2026, compared to October 2025. But, this result was weighed down. October 2026 had one fewer sales day than last year, Kirkland said. In reality, the receipts from existing-home sales were down 2.7% in October 2026 compared to October 2025.

Liebowitz attributed many of the Q3 losses to changes, and called it a “growth stage.”

Kirkland claimed the company would see returns on its current investments—such as the development marketing pipeline of $26 billion and the additional $11.8 billion scheduled to come to market Dec. 31, 2027—between 2026 and 2032. In particular, Kirkland mentioned Florida’s real estate market and its marketing value.

“We see positive indicators within our development marketing business in Florida, with approximately $19.5 billion gross transaction value, of the $26 billion of gross transaction value that is being actively marketed,” he added. “For most projects in Florida, we receive progress payments during the marketing process and defer the related revenue and commission it spent until the earnings process is complete, which is when the underlying sale closes.”

After investing in an “AI transformation” last quarter, the Q3 earnings release noted that the initiative is expected to gradually drive significant savings in non-commission operating expenses over the next three years.

“Modernizing those systems should make the company more efficient while giving our agents and employees better tools and more time to focus on clients, relationships and growing their businesses,” Liebowitz claimed. “That work is underway, and we remain focused on gradually realizing meaningful efficiencies in our non-commission operating expenses beginning in 2027.”

#5602. Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades

Anthropic PBC today pulled back the curtains on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two most capable large language models to date.

The LLMs are identical as far as their core capabilities are concerned. The difference is that Fable 5.2 blocks certain biology and cybersecurity use cases, while Mythos 5.2 includes more relaxed guardrails. The latter model is only available to trusted researchers through a pair of limited-access programs.

Anthropic tested Fable 5.2 against its predecessor across 14 artificial intelligence benchmarks. The model beat Fable 5.1’s score by more than 10% across most of the tests. It’s particularly adept at scientific research: Fable 5.2 scored 74.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a 22% improvement over Fable 5.1.

Earlier this year, Anthropic used an unreleased LLM to generate a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The project took 11 days. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 reduced the workflow to 30 hours by spinning up 1,000 agents to parallelize calculations. In a separate project, it answered two open questions about a theoretical physics concept related to black holes.

The company also tested Mythos 5.2, the invite-only version of Fable 5.2. It asked the model to study the protective shells of harmless viruses called AAVs. AAV shells, or capsids as they’re known in scientific parlance, are used by some therapies to deliver drugs.

Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled the structure of 28 out of the 34 AAV capsids it studied. The result is notable because capsids comprise dozens of different proteins. Other cutting-edge models that are optimized for biology research, notably Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold2, can only model the structure of individual proteins. The creators of the latter model won one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block most research biology questions and many cybersecurity-related prompts. If users enter a request that falls into either of those categories, the model sends it to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1.

The model outperforms its predecessor by more than 13% across two coding benchmarks called FrontierCode 2.0 FrontierSWE 2.0. According to Anthropic, one of its engineers put the model’s programming capabilities to the test by asking it to build an operating system. Fable 5.2 spun up up 1,000 agents that completed the task in about eight days. The operating system they created can run on a laptop, offers network access and features a Claude sidebar.

Anthropic sees customers using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 to speed up highly complicated, open-ended technical tasks. The company says more day-to-day workflows can be automated more efficiently using Opus 5.5, an LLM it introduced in July. Users can also combine the models by having Opus 5.5 ask Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 for advise when it encounters a bottleneck.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That makes them 20% more affordable than Anthropic’s previous-generation models. Both LLMs offer a high-performance mode that generates prompt responses 2.5 times faster than the standard tier for double the price.

#5601. Las Vegas Inventory Hits Record High as Buyer Demand Sinks—but One Surprising Segment Defies the Slump

Housing inventory in Las Vegas surged to an all-time high in October as high mortgage rates priced out everyday buyers, yet the luxury tier of the local market continued to outperform.

Active listings in Nevada's largest metro jumped nearly 10% year over year, reaching 11,447 units—the highest level on record for Realtor.com® data going back to July 2016, according to the October housing market report.

Tania Jhayem, a real estate agent at Keller Williams The Marketplace's luxury division in Las Vegas, says that mortgage rates exceeding 7% and broader affordability headwinds have encouraged buyers to be far more selective.

"After several years of an extremely competitive housing market, we're seeing a shift toward more balanced conditions, where buyers have additional choices and sellers are adjusting to a different pace," Jhayem tells Realtor.com.

New listings—a measure of fresh homes hitting the market—plunged 10.5% compared to last year, further underscoring a wider market cooldown.

Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel notes that new listings accounted for less than a quarter of the overall inventory in October compared to 30.4% a year ago. The result is an inventory that is growing increasingly stale.

The typical for-sale home in Las Vegas lingered on the market for 59 days last month, two days longer than during the same period in 2025.

While the selection for sale may not be the freshest this fall—with half of the available homes sitting on the market for nearly two months—the buildup offers buyers a key advantage: time.

"Buyers who previously felt priced out or pressured into quick decisions now have more opportunities to explore their options," says Jhayem. "For sellers, proper pricing, presentation, and marketing have become increasingly important. Ultimately, we're seeing a market where both buyers and sellers are becoming more deliberate in their decisions."

Homes lingering on the market present well-prepared shoppers with opportunities to negotiate favorable terms, including price cuts, closing-cost assistance, repairs, or mortgage rate buydowns.

This fall, house hunters can also take their time to evaluate properties, review comparable sales, and make informed decisions without the intense pressure seen in recent years.

Yet, a prolonged listing history does not always spell a bargain: Some homes require major updates, have features that appeal to a small pool of would-be buyers, or are simply mispriced.

The record-setting inventory buildup was not an overnight development. Data analysis reveals that active listings in Las vegas have climbed steadily since January.

"That's a massive part of what's going on in markets like Vegas—not just in October but over the last several months as rates have risen and erased the financing advantage that buyers had enjoyed for much of this year compared to last," notes Krimmel.

The median asking price in Las Vegas registered at $459,900 in October, down 2.6% year over year but still nearly $45,000 higher than the national price. Meanwhile, contract signings were down by more than 25% year over year, outpacing the 17% decline recorded nationally.

Despite the slowdown, sellers are keeping their cool: Roughly 24% of all listings in Vegas saw price reductions, down 1.4 percentage points from last year. Mirroring the broader national trend, the dip suggests that sellers are in no rush to hand out concessions just to offload properties.

"Many of the homeowners choosing to sell today are doing so because of important life transitions rather than simply reacting to market conditions," says the Vegas agent. "We're seeing reasons to sell that include job relocations, growing families, retirees looking to downsize, estate settlements, and homeowners seeking properties that better fit their current lifestyles."

Jhayem points out that one of the important differences between today's market and previous downturns is that many local homeowners have built substantial equity, which provides greater flexibility and allows sellers to make more strategic decisions about when and how to sell.

"Homeowners with favorable mortgage rates and no immediate need to move may choose to stay put, while those ready for their next chapter are continuing to move forward," she adds.

While the broader Las Vegas housing market cooled, the upper tier heated up.

The entry threshold for the top 10% of the metro's housing market reached $1.2 million in October, up 2.2% from a year ago, marking the 10th-biggest price growth among the 43 largest metros, according to the latest Realtor.com luxury housing report.

According to Krimmel, this divergence stems from two market dynamics: robust demand from wealthy, well-capitalized buyers who are less sensitive to high mortgage rates, and the resilience of the luxury tier buoyed by sellers who can afford to wait for their target sale price.

"While the general market is maybe kind of softening, the ultraluxury market ... there's no breaks in store for it," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com.

Harris points out that so far in 2026, there have been 23 properties in Vegas that were sold for over $10 million, with two more under contract. This is up from the 18 that were sold in that price range all of last year.

The adviser attributes this trend in part to Nevada's tax-friendly climate and pro-business policies, which continue to draw a steady stream of what she jokingly calls "refugees" from higher-taxation markets in California and Washington.

The other part of the equation, according to Harris, is the evolution of Las Vegas from a weekend gambling getaway destination into a prestigious sports and entertainment capital.

Jhayem agrees, stressing that year to year, Las Vegas continues to demonstrate its appeal as a luxury hub drawing deep-pocketed buyers relocating for lifestyle upgrades, tax considerations, and long-term investment goals.

"Our city offers an exceptional combination of luxury living, entertainment, dining, outdoor recreation, and relative value compared with many other major metropolitan areas," she says.

While rising luxury asking-price thresholds are an encouraging indication of the market's positioning, high-end properties are still taking longer to sell compared to average homes.

In October, the median days on the market for a luxury listing reached 73, a full week slower than a year ago. According to Jhayem, the longer wait time comes down to high net worth buyers being increasingly selective and placing a greater emphasis on quality, location, and value.

"Overall, I see Las Vegas transitioning toward a more balanced, opportunity-driven market," concludes the agent. "Buyers have greater choice and negotiating power, while sellers who approach the market strategically can still achieve successful outcomes. Today's market is less about urgency and more about making informed decisions."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5600. ‘Home Is Where You Spend’: How Your Neighborhood Shapes Your Buying Habits

Your home isn't just where you live; it's also where you spend the majority of your money, a new study from financial technology platform Bilt has found.

Bilt partnered with 451 Research and S&P Global on the 2026 State of the Neighborhood survey, aimed at exploring consumer spending habits as it doubles down on American business with the launch of Bilt Neighborhood OS and the expansion of its membership platform.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is an AI operating system and commerce network designed to unlock America's $6.6 trillion neighborhood commerce opportunity to help businesses grow without replacing their existing systems, the company says.

In the consumer spending survey, around two-thirds of the 6,951 survey participants conducted at least 80% of their "everyday spending" within 15 miles of their homes, and 92% of those surveyed planned on spending the same or more at local businesses in the coming months.

That's not surprising, given the results of a recent Re/Max survey, which found that 29% of prospective homeowners valued proximity to grocery stores and shopping, while 20% said they valued having restaurants and cafes nearby.

More than half of all survey respondents said future neighborhood development, including new housing or retail development, was "very important" to how they chose where to buy a home.

The results of the Bilt survey spell good news for small businesses in popular residential areas, suggesting that physical stores close to dense residential neighborhoods may continue to thrive in the age of online shopping.

"The disconnect between what people talk about versus where people actually spend is quite significant," Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt, tells Realtor.com®. "When you you look at the stats, all online shopping in the U.S. is $1.3 trillion a year. But offline, small- and medium-business local retail and food spending is $6.6 trillion."

On a quarterly basis, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, that broke down to $340.2 billion in online spending in the second quarter, making up 17.1% of total consumer spending.

Bilt's study found that 70% of food and grocery spending is still made in person.

Consumers spent an average of $375 on in-person grocery shopping each month. They spent an additional $175 on in-person dining and takeout and another $175 on in-person general shopping. Study participants reported spending an average of $50 each on entertainment and recreation; health and personal care; and transportation.

Sixty-six percent of survey respondents said they were were actively looking to support local businesses over big-box and online retailers and were willing to spend more to support them.

A recent report on consumer spending habits around the holidays from research firm Epsilon found that Gen Z in particular values in-store options for gift shopping. And while online shopping is still, overall, the preferred method for gift shopping, the study found that consumers across all generatios are doing the majority of their food and decoration shopping in person. Furthermore, they spent about an equal amount of their holiday clothing budgets online and in store.

One possible reason for the continued primacy of in-person shopping is consumers' paradoxical relationship with artificial intelligence marketing.

Research from McKinsey found that AI continues to drive sales and that AI usage in completing purchases climbed 70% year over year. However, younger, more tech-native shoppers "tend to be more skeptical of AI on average," the report found. (Sixty-seven percent of American Gen Z AI users trust AI chat and search tools versus the global average of 73%.)

The study was conducted in advance of Bilt launching its new offerings. Alongside Bilt Neighborhood OS, the Bilt Membership Platform is an expansion of the company's existing membership and loyalty technology. The company says it will enable organizations to launch their own branded membership programs via white-labeling or extend existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood.

"We are betting pretty big on the neighborhood versus online commerce," Jain says. "There is a huge gap between what the media and the Silicon Valley world talk about versus how real Americans are living. People talk about AI as 'How are we going to do online commerce AI and replace coding and jobs and all this stuff.'

"The truth is, the biggest beneficiaries of AI can be the local mom and pop businesses who don't have the ability to hire 2,000 people to go compete with, like, a Walmart or Amazon online.

"Everything is tied together. The more you can invest in the neighborhood, the more value you create in the housing. The more housing you have, the more you can invest in the neighborhood," he adds.

Bilt also announced a coalition of partners spanning payments, point-of-sale technology, reservations, and commerce platforms. Partners include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Bungalow Hospitality Management, ByNext, FlyBox, Lettuce Entertain You, Lowe’s, Prince Street Hospitality Group, The Dinex Group, Thumbtack, among others.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5599. Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents

Meta Platforms Inc. today introduced Muse Ember, an entry-level artificial intelligence model that costs significantly less than the competition.

Notably, it’s the first AI that the company trained using Muse Wonder. The latter algorithm is the Facebook parent’s flagship large language model. Meta didn’t specify which part of the workflow it automated with Muse Wonder.

One possibility is that the company used it to perform post-training, the task of honing a model’s capabilities by training it on additional data. Thinking Machines Labs Inc. recently demonstrated that even a relatively small LLM can run post-training runs end-to-end. Anthropic PBC, for its part, last week revealed that its AI models could soon gain the ability to significantly accelerate machine learning research.

Applications often use frontier LLMs such as Muse Wonder as part of AI ensembles. When a user enters a request, the frontier LLM splits it into smaller tasks and assigns them to agents powered by a lower-cost model. Meta says Muse Ember is specifically optimized to play the latter role.

The company evaluated the model using the Artificial Analysis Index, which aggregates nine AI benchmarks spanning use cases such as coding and financial analysis. Meta says that Muse Ember matched the score of Anthropic’s entry-level Claude Haiku 5.5 model at about a third the price. It also outperformed OpenAI Group PBC’s comparable GPT-6 Luna algorithm.

The same internal evaluation saw Meta test Muse Ember and the two rival models across nine other benchmarks. All three algorithms were in “max” mode, which means they used the maximum amount of hardware at their disposal instead of prioritizing cost-efficiency. Muse Ember outperformed Haiku and Luna across seven of the benchmarks.

The area where the model appears to have the biggest edge is business task automation. Whereas most of Muse Ember’s benchmark results were only a few percentage points better than those of Haiku and Luna, it clocked a 17% lead on AutomationBench-AA. It’s a collection of 657 tasks that span popular cloud applications such as Gmail and Salesforce.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens, which enables it to ingest lengthy business documents. Users can also include images, audio and video in their prompts. The model generates responses up to 512,000 tokens in length.

Muse Ember is available through Meta’s Model API for 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens. A built-in cache can reuse frequently used prompts to avoid duplicate processing. When the feature is active, Muse Ember’s pricing drops to 0.4 cents per million input tokens.

#5598. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5597. California Voters Reject ‘Billionaires Tax’ Amid Fears of an Exodus of Wealth From the State

California voters have rejected a proposed wealth tax, which could have meant a one-time influx of billions for the state but threatened to trigger an exodus of billionaires in the state.

The ballot measure, one of several housing issues Californians considered, is projected by the Associated Press to narrowly fail, with 53% voting against the measure with most votes counted a week after Election Day. Proposition 40 would have created a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals with a net worth above $1 billion.

The Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the measure, said it could have offset federal funding cuts. It estimated the one time tax could have brought in $100 billion in one-time revenue.

But the measure could have affected about 200 people, and billionaires in the state have put significant money toward fighting it. The California Budget & Policy Center estimates they hold a combined $2 trillion in wealth. Proposition 40 excludes real property holdings from determining an individual's net worth.

State leaders say tax could trigger some of those wealthy people to flee the state and take their spending with them. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimates California could collect $40 billion from the tax. But it could lose $25 billion in other taxes if wealthy people leave.

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the measure. "This will be defeated, there's no question in my mind," Newsom told the New York Times, as it reported that several wealthy people had begun moving assets out of the state.

Palantir and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin all have reportedly moved some assets to Florida. Voters in that state approved a measure on Tuesday that would reform its property tax system, potentially setting it up to be yet more attractive.

However, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had pledged to remain in California, where he has spent more than $112 million assembling a megacompound in Palo Alto. Earlier this year, Zuckerberg reached an agreement with the Meta board to remain in California regardless of the outcome of Prop 40. He would have faced a potential tax bill of some $12.5 billion if the measure had passed.

Taxes raised by Prop 40 would have gone to health care, education, or food assistance. But the state legislature would have had discretion to determine how those funds are used.

The California Association of Realtors President Tamara Suminski said at an elections forum last month that it opposed the measure. CAR is concerned about the potential loss of tax revenue and the state's economic competitiveness, she said.

"Prop 40 is just a bad idea," Jennifer Barrera, president & CEO, California Chamber of Commerce, said at the event. "Billionaires are the individuals who have the ability to move quickly, they have the ability to live outside the state, they don't have to be in California. And yet they pay a tremendous amount of revenue to our general fund if they're living here."

Two other items on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42 both aimed to block or counter Proposition 40, but their language could have had much broader implications, Barrera said.

But even if Proposition 40 had passed, it would have invited years of litigation, said Joe Bishop‐​Henchman, executive vice president at National Taxpayers Union Foundation. Prop 40 applied to all of a California-domiciled billionaire's holdings across the globe, inviting Constitutional challenges.

And then there's the matter of actually calculating net worth. Wealthy individuals hold assets that can be hard to value, such as patents, artwork, and stakes in private companies. So, it would have likely taken years of expensive legal process to determine how much to tax them.

"The Franchise Tax Board currently has no infrastructure for valuing these types of assets," Bishop‐​Henchman said. "Valuing these kinds of assets will entail years of costly litigation on both ends and establishment of an extensive and costly administrative apparatus for an ostensibly 'one-time' tax."

Californians, meanwhile, also voted on a set of other measures. Voters passed Proposition 1 to authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs. Co-chairs of its organizing campaign, Chione Flegal and Ray Pearl, called the win "a resounding show of support for affordable housing."

Voters also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income buyers to purchase new homes. Realtor.com® economist Joel Berner says this could be a boon for new-home sales. But he cautioned it might not touch the more expensive parts of the state.

"The complicating factor here is that the major California metro areas are short on newly built homes below $1.5 million, and the ballot measure does nothing to address the supply of these homes, only bolstering demand for them," Berner says.

"Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy," he notes.

The California Association of Realtors, a major supporter of Proposition 37, cheered the result.

“This measure will help create more housing, provide low-cost down payment options and give teachers, nurses, firefighters and other hardworking Californians a better opportunity to own a home in the communities they serve," Suminski said. "We look forward to working with stakeholders to bring Proposition 37 to life and deliver on its promise for California families.”

But, voters rejected the controversial Proposition 45. It would have set timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA.

California earned an F grade on the Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card. It tracks how effectively each state balances affordability and new construction.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5596. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

#5595. Inflation Remains Hot in October and Strengthens Case for Another Fed Rate Hike

Inflation accelerated faster than anticipated in October, driven by surging costs for housing and food, which will bolster the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.

On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Tuesday. That's down from the 0.6% monthly increase recorded in September but higher than the 0.2% gain forecasted by economists.

CPI measures the average costs consumers pay for a range of goods, including food, energy, commodities, and services.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3%, also exceeding the anticipated 0.2% gain.

The BLS did not publish an official annual inflation rate because last year's government shutdown prevented the agency from collecting survey data for October 2025.

October saw the index for shelter jump 0.3%, accounting for over 30% of the monthly all-items increase. Meanwhile, the food index increased 0.5%, and the energy index rose 0.7%, coming on the heels of a 5.2% surge in September.

Prices for a wide range of goods and services, including recreation, transportation, medical care, vehicle insurance, education, airfare, and tariff-sensitive categories like furniture and apparel all increased in October.

"These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel.

The October CPI print, coupled with the better-than-expected jobs number released last week, signals for the Federal Reserve that it must continue focusing its efforts on combating inflation.

At last month's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its current 3.75%-4% range.

However, a December hike now looks all but certain, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase climbing to 99% Tuesday morning, before settling back down to 85%, according to CME FedWatch.

Krimmel says that market reaction is both due to the warmer-than-anticipated CPI print and Fed Gov. Christopher Waller’s latest comments.

Speaking before the inflation report release, Waller put a 50-basis-point move on the table for December and stressed the need to follow through on market expectations for rate increases.

"When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out," said Waller.

Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury going up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI release.

For housing in the near term, Krimmel says the rising yields and growing speculation about future interest rate increases could put upward pressure on mortgage rates again, reversing a recent downward trend that saw the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifting to 7.18% last week.

October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back from the market.

And while rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand.

Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7%.

#5594. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5593. PitchBook opens its platform to startups for free and debuts Origin deal sourcing service

Private markets data provider PitchBook Data Inc. today opened its platform to startups for free at Web Summit in Lisbon.

Those that sign up have to share their financials. Some of that information will reach investors through the company’s new deal sourcing service, PitchBook Origin.

The launches come as more startups than ever are landing a first round. In the U.S., the 2021 record for first-time financings had already fallen by the end of September, PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association found in their latest Venture Monitor report.

PitchBook credits artificial intelligence with part of that growth, since the technology has made companies easier to start. AI tools have also compressed investor diligence from weeks to days. Sourcing has not kept pace, the company argues, particularly where the signals are not public.

Free access for startups runs through a program called PitchBook for Startups. Founders who have bootstrapped or raised only from angels, grants or accelerators qualify as long as they are now seeking a first institutional round and can show at least a mockup of their product.

Once a startup has handed over its financials and details on its leadership team and product, its founders can use the PitchBook platform to research which firms are actively writing checks in their sector and stage. Investor research tops PitchBook’s own list of what founders can do with the access.

That founder data lands in a much bigger pool on the Origin side, where coverage starts at about 25 million companies and 250 million people profiles. Bootstrapped businesses and companies that have not yet raised money or announced what they are building are part of that count, and some 15 million of the companies are new to PitchBook.

Third-party data enrichment and PitchBook’s own machine learning models supply part of the coverage. PitchBook said it has not had founder-verified data at scale before.

Each company gets a score, and investors can tune relevance filters to their own criteria. Real-time alerts, saved searches and customer relationship management integrations are meant to replace the manual monitoring that deal teams do now.

Chief Solutions Officer Paul Santarelli said the missing piece for investors has been visibility into “the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see.” Every company that joins the startup program and contributes verified information sharpens that picture, he said.

PitchBook “was once a startup itself, working to get in front of the right backers,” President and Chief Operating Officer Rod Diefendorf said. Founded in 2007, the Seattle company now serves more than 100,000 clients worldwide. Morningstar Inc. has owned it since 2016.

Startups can apply for the program now. Origin is available as a standalone product or as an add-on to the main PitchBook platform.

#5591. Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC Connect Florida and Indiana Property Data Through RPR View

Business professional using laptop with connected digital document icons, representing document management, data sharing, cloud workflow, file organization, and business automation.

Realtors Property Resource (RPR) has announced that Realtors serving clients with real estate interests in both Florida and Indiana will have access to additional property information through a new data-sharing collaboration between Stellar MLS and MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative (BLC).

According to a release, using RPR View, the MLS data-sharing capability from RPR, eligible customers in both markets will be able to access approved off-market listings, including historical listing data, across MLS boundaries.

RPR says the collaboration reflects a natural connection between Indiana and Florida, where seasonal residents, relocating homeowners and buyers often have real estate interests in both markets. Expanded access to listing history gives Realtors additional context to research properties, understand past market activity and help clients make informed decisions.

“Buyers and sellers deserve informed guidance wherever their real estate goals take them,” said Shayne Fairley, CEO of Stellar MLS. “Often, they don’t stop at market boundaries, and neither should access to trusted listing information for the real estate professionals who serve them. With strong ties between Florida and Indiana, especially among seasonal residents, our collaboration with MIBOR BLC and RPR will provide greater access to property information across both markets, so the professionals who guide their clients can do so with greater confidence.”

He added: “We’re pleased to bring this expanded access to our collective customers, and we look forward to creating similar opportunities with other MLSs and associations.”

A practical approach to cross-market data sharing

Beyond the benefits to Realtors, the release says the collaboration demonstrates how MLS organizations can expand property data access using technology already available through RPR.

With RPR View, participating MLSs determine which listing information to share and which markets can access it. This gives organizations flexibility to expand access while maintaining control over their data-sharing permissions.

For Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC, the arrangement enables reciprocal access to approved off-market listing information, including historical listing data, through an established platform, without developing a separate data-sharing system.

“MLS organizations create the greatest value when we look beyond traditional market boundaries and focus on how real estate professionals actually do business. Our partnership with Stellar MLS reflects that philosophy,” said Shelley Specchio, CEO and President of the MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative in Indiana. “By connecting the Indiana and Florida marketplaces through RPR, we are reducing friction for professionals working in both states and demonstrating what is possible when MLSs collaborate around the needs of brokers, agents and consumers.”

Building connections through existing infrastructure

The release notes that as of October 31, 341 of the nation’s 487 MLSs (70%) participate in RPR View data sharing, representing more than 1 million Realtors. The Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC collaboration demonstrates how this existing infrastructure can support cross-market access while allowing each organization to maintain control over its shared data, RPR says.

“One of the advantages of RPR View is that MLSs can expand data access without having to build a new solution,” said Liz Gunski, vice president of Industry Relations at RPR. “Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC are showing how existing infrastructure can support collaboration while keeping participating organizations in control of their data.”

The expanded data access is scheduled to become available to eligible customers in both markets beginning Nov. 4.

#5590. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. #5588. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5587. AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run

Israeli artificial intelligence security startup Bay AI Inc. launched today with $50 million in funding to let enterprises vet each action an AI agent tries to take before it runs.

Bay provides software that tracks the agents working across a company, whether they sit on an employee’s laptop, inside a cloud workload or in a software-as-a-service application. One set of policies covers them all.

First-generation AI security tools mostly filter prompts and responses. Bay argues that misses where the damage happens, since a harmless-looking prompt can still end with an agent deleting a production database.

The founders ran into that kind of failure themselves when one of their own coding agents, working with its normal permissions, tried to expose a cloud environment to the internet to finish a test. They still have the screenshot.

Bay installs through the mobile device management or endpoint detection and response tools a customer already has, and the company says it takes under five minutes. A scanner called Wave inventories the agents, extensions and local models on each machine and leaves nothing running once it finishes.

Each time an agent proposes an action, the AI tool running it hands the request to Bay Enforcer, a static binary, through a native hook. The check happens on the machine itself with the whole session as context, and Bay said a verdict comes back in milliseconds, sometimes as a prompt asking the user to approve the step. Anything judged too risky never runs.

The policy behind those verdicts comes from Bay’s Lighthouse system, which drafts a separate one for each team from the last 30 days of agent activity, so security staff are not writing rules every time someone picks up a new tool. Teams can test a policy against the previous month first and see what it would have stopped. Bay said false positives run under 1%.

Security leaders are often handed an enterprise-wide AI rollout with a year-end deadline, co-founder and Chief Executive Yuval Zacharia said, or find that agents have already spread across the company and “it’s the Wild West.” She wants security to become “the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”

Micron Technology Inc., Wix.com Ltd., ClickUp Inc. and Peloton Interactive Inc. are among the dozens of enterprise customers signed in the nine months since Bay was founded. Fortune 100 companies on the platform tripled their use of autonomous agents in just under 30 days, the company said.

Zacharia founded Bay with Chief Product Officer Aner Morag and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich. The three knew each other from the Israel Defense Forces’ Unit 8200, where Zacharia led a department of about 50 people before becoming the first intelligence officer there to cross into offensive cyber operations. After the military she ran security research and AI at Cyber Hunters Ltd.

Danilovich was an early employee at Preempt Security Inc. and stayed six years at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. after it bought the startup in 2020. Most of Bay’s research team followed him over. Morag was the first employee at Noname Security.

The $50 million comes from two rounds. Battery Ventures LP led the larger $37 million Series A round, and Micron’s venture arm, Micron Ventures, also participated after the chipmaker started out as a Bay customer. Wiz Inc. Chief Executive Assaf Rappaport put in money personally. The remaining $13 million came from a previously undisclosed seed round co-led by YL Ventures Ltd. and Striker Venture Partners.

Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures, said his firm looked at a crowded field of AI endpoint security companies before picking Bay. He believes it can become “as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”

Engineering and product hiring will continue in Tel Aviv, where Bay is based, with the sales, marketing and customer teams growing in the U.S. and Europe. Enterprises can buy the platform now.

#5586. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

While speaking to The Perfect Magazine, the actress, 52, revealed that she and Bardem, 57, opted to bring their son Leo, 15, and daughter Luna, 12, up in Madrid because it allows them to live a more private lifestyle.

#5584. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5583. Teleport makes Beams generally available to bring AI agents into production

Infrastructure identity company Teleport today made Teleport Beams, its runtime for artificial intelligence agents that work on production infrastructure, generally available.

Beams goes after what Teleport sees as the main reason agents have stayed out of production so far. Most enterprises have not plugged agents into those systems at all, according to Ev Kontsevoy, Teleport’s co-founder and chief executive. He blamed gaps such as delegated identity and an audit trail that follows an agent from intent to action.

Sandboxes, the tool many teams reach for now, mostly isolate the agent in a virtual machine and handle its credentials. “When the cost of an error is high, traditional sandboxes don’t cut it,” Kontsevoy said ahead of the announcement.

Teleport calls each individual runtime a Beam, and every agent gets its own. A Beam carries a delegated identity inherited from the user or agent that launched it, while the agent inside starts with no standing privileges. Work begins with a proposed execution plan. That plan can be revised by a person or by a large language model acting as judge before a separate Beam runs it with only the approved roles. Reviewers then see new requests only for steps outside the plan.

Passwords never enter the agent’s environment. Everything the agent sends to a model is traced, and Teleport says that record lets Beams pick out a hijacked goal or agents coordinating in ways nobody planned. Each session also gets scored against the MITRE ATT&CK framework for a written risk summary. Seven of the detection rules come prebuilt, privilege escalation among them. Anything else a customer wants caught can be described in natural language and added to the set.

Each Beam is an ephemeral micro-VM on a virtualized network. Nothing gets in or out without passing Teleport’s controls, and the audit log keeps a copy of every protocol exchange. Snapshots taken by a feature named Phases carry the files and memory of an expiring Beam into the next one, so longer jobs do not have to start over.

Teams can also fork a Beam to try several approaches in parallel. When something goes badly wrong, a kill switch ends the agent’s activity and cuts all of its connections to production at once.

Teleport makes no promise about what a model will decide. A hijacked or mistaken agent inside a Beam can reach only what it was granted until its authority lapses at the end of the task, and every action it takes stays on the record.

Beams runs on top of the Teleport Infrastructure Identity Platform, which the company says is in production at more than 700 enterprises, Nasdaq Inc., DoorDash Inc. and Elastic N.V. among them. Cisco Systems Inc. became Teleport’s largest strategic investor in August.

Teleport first showed Beams in March, two months after publishing the Teleport Agentic Identity Framework that the runtime now puts into practice. Following a public beta, the product is available at beams.run.
