#5582. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5580. The VA Home Loan Benefits Giving Military Buyers an Edge in a Tough Market

Thanks to the bravery and sacrifices of our veterans and active military, our country’s civilians can live the American dream in safety. So how fitting is it that one tangible way our country says "thank you for your service" to current and former members of the military is through the Department of Veterans Affairs home loan benefit?

These unique mortgage options allow veterans and those still serving to acquire their own piece of the American dream by potentially qualifying for homes they might have otherwise thought were out of reach.

In July 2025, HR 1815, the VA Home Loan Reform Act, passed with bipartisan support through the House, Senate, and President Donald Trump.

Backed by the National Association of Realtors®, the bill made permanent a policy allowing veterans to directly pay their real estate agents—ensuring equal access to the housing market. It also establishes a partial claims program to help veterans catch up on missed mortgage payments.

"The VA Home Loan Guaranty is a unique government program that allows veterans to purchase a home without a down payment," said Shannon McGahn, NAR executive vice president and chief advocacy officer at the time.

"We are grateful to the House of Representatives and the Senate for passing this measure and providing veterans and active-duty service members the same advantages as other buyers in a competitive real estate market. NAR remains committed to protecting the brave men and women who serve this country in the armed forces and ensuring they are given equal opportunities to achieve the American dream of homeownership."

Veterans, active-duty service personnel, and select reservists or National Guard members are among those who can qualify for VA loans (find eligibility requirements here). Wondering what some of the benefits of a VA loan might be? Here are five of the most popular features.

This is one of the most valuable and touted benefits—and for good reason. Saving enough for a down payment can be the biggest obstacle to buying a home. But a VA loan eliminates that roadblock.

“Most of the buyers I work with don’t have extra resources available, so the fact that they can purchase a home with zero down makes the transaction feasible,” says Benny Dinsmore, himself a veteran and a real estate agent with Coldwell Banker in Frisco, TX.

Qualified VA buyers don’t have a down payment requirement in most cases.

But beware: The “no money down” aspect of a VA loan shouldn’t be confused with “no money out of pocket,” a common misconception, notes Michael Garcia, broker and owner of Weichert, Realtors–TQS in Lake Worth, FL.

A VA purchase transaction still requires closing costs and often includes an earnest money deposit (a negotiated amount of money that the buyer puts in escrow to essentially "hold" the house).

“However, that money will often come back at the closing, when the title company will write a check back to the veteran on the spot for the total amount that was put into escrow,” Garcia says.

The required credit score for a VA loan can be lower than for a conventional loan—around 620 for a VA loan compared with a range of 650 to 700 for most conventional loans.

In addition, the required debt-to-income ratio for VA loans is often more flexible than for conventional mortgages.

“It allows someone with less-than-perfect credit and some debt to still be able to qualify for a loan,” Dinsmore says.

Most conventional buyers have to pay private mortgage insurance if they put less than 20% down. Federal Housing Administration loans come with their own forms of mortgage insurance. But a VA loan waives that insurance requirement.

"This can be a big savings in monthly payments," says real estate agent Twila Lukavich, with Russell Real Estate Services in Cleveland.

Even though there's no mortgage insurance, there is a "funding fee"—an upfront cost applied to every purchase loan or refinance. The proceeds help the VA cover losses on the few loans that go into default. But borrowers can roll it into their monthly payment, or pay it all at once. Plus, it's tax-deductible. And veterans with a service-connected disability and select others don’t have to pay the funding fee at all.

Legally, veterans might have to pay for certain closing costs, which include the following:

But there are some fees that veterans don't have to pay. And the VA allows lenders to charge no more than 1% to cover the costs of originating and underwriting the loan.

Furthermore, even those costs can be rolled into the loan. So, for example, if the purchase price is $280,000, the veteran might offer $300,000 and ask for 3% back to cover the closing costs.

“In this way, the veteran is essentially financing their closing costs into the loan, meaning less out of pocket at the start,” Dinsmore explains.

When a home that a veteran is considering purchasing is having trouble reaching the purchase price during the appraisal process, buyers and lenders can ask the VA appraiser to consider adjusting the valuation before making a final determination.

Appraisers notify lenders in the event the appraised value is likely to come in low, giving buyers and real estate agents 48 hours to supply additional information that the appraiser might not be aware of to help justify the home’s value.

"Typically, I assemble an itemized list of upgrades and improvements that the seller has performed on the home in the past three years that the appraiser didn’t know about, and therefore didn’t include in the home value," Lukavich says.

This process "gives the agents an opportunity to assist the appraiser in making sure they have the whole picture of the home and gives the local agent an opening to help an appraiser be educated on specific local values,” she adds.

It's just another benefit of VA loans aimed at helping our servicemen/women buy the home of their dreams.

Cathie Ericson writes about real estate, finance, and health. She lives in Portland, OR.

#5579. Commvault unveils Recovery Studio, AgentRecover update and joint work with three partners

Data protection provider Commvault Systems Inc. today used its SHIFT 2026 customer event to unveil Recovery Studio, a new service that will automate the rebuilding of entire business applications after an outage or cyberattack.

Four other announcements cover recovery for artificial intelligence agents and joint work with Databricks Inc., Nvidia Corp. and Zscaler Inc.

AgentRecover, the company’s tool for reversing damage done by AI agents, is being extended to agents built on Microsoft Corp.’s Foundry and on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from Amazon Web Services Inc. Databricks and Nvidia technology will draw on governed enterprise data from Commvault’s Data Activate service. The Zscaler agreement is a strategic partnership centered on AI security.

Recovery Studio goes after the manual work of restoring a business one piece at a time. Data alone does not get an application running again. Without the identities, configurations and infrastructure it depends on, an application can stay offline long after its files are back.

A large enterprise may have hundreds of applications and thousands of identities to bring up in sequence. Getting back to even a minimal level of operation takes 28 days on average under conventional approaches, according to Commvault research from last year.

In place of that manual work, the service uses automated runbooks that rebuild and validate each component in order. Commvault said the runbooks also restore identity systems and cloud configurations, firewall rules included. Threat scans can run inside a runbook on supported resources, and the results feed into the call on whether a service is ready to go back into production. Operational, disaster and cyber recovery all run from the same platform.

Pranay Ahlawat, Commvault’s chief technology and AI officer, called the launch “the DevOps moment for recovery.” He said one orchestrated flow can take over from the spreadsheets and war rooms that recovery teams lean on today.

The AgentRecover update moves the company’s agent protection onto the platforms where businesses build production agents. In September Commvault added protection for agent configurations that tools such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code store on employee laptops.

Phil Goodwin, research vice president at International Data Corp., said conventional recovery assumes a discrete set of data at one point in time. Agents break that assumption, because the agent, its data and the resources around it all have to come back “at machine speed,” he said.

On Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry, the software discovers each agent and maps the data, applications and infrastructure it interacts with. If an agent goes rogue, its activity log shows which systems it may have touched across platforms.

Restores target the agent and whatever it changed. Customers can also run AgentRecover with Commvault’s identity recovery and change auditing tools to trace the identities an agent acted through.

The Databricks and Nvidia announcements both build on Data Activate, which turns backup copies protected by Commvault into datasets for analytics and AI. Much of the data companies hold is unstructured and scattered across systems. In research from BARC published by DataHub in June, 70% of data and AI leaders said less than half of their unstructured data could be found and used for AI.

Commvault Data Activate for Databricks shares data under Commvault management into Databricks through OpenSharing. The data arrives as governed tables in Unity Catalog with its ownership, access permissions and lineage intact.

Updates keep flowing as source content changes or is deleted, and customers do not have to rebuild a connection to every original source. Alan Atkinson, chief business development officer at Commvault, said the aim is “turning protected data into an active business asset.”

Nvidia’s part, delivered as a reference design for software-as-a-service and software deployments, centers on retrieval. Nvidia NIM microservices and Nemotron Retriever, together with the Nvidia cuVS library used with Apache Solr, extract and organize Commvault-protected content so applications and agents can pull from it more easily. Data Activate keeps that content current as source files change, retention periods expire or permissions are revoked.

On the security side, Commvault and Zscaler listed AI discovery, runtime governance and agent detection and recovery as early areas of collaboration, and the companies did not announce a joint product or availability date. Zscaler’s Security for AI line polices how employees and agents use AI tools. Dhawal Sharma, Zscaler’s executive vice president of AI security and strategic initiatives, said organizations need to be “prepared to recover quickly if something goes wrong.”

Recovery Studio, AgentRecover’s Amazon Bedrock AgentCore support and the Databricks integration are all due to enter early access in December, the last of them in select Microsoft Azure regions. Foundry support comes sooner, with early access targeted for this month.

The Nvidia reference design is set to reach general availability in 2027 after an early release in December. Recovery Studio will be priced on the amount of data configured for orchestrated recovery, and Commvault plans general availability in the coming months.

A virtual edition of SHIFT follows on Nov. 18.

#5578. Lumbra gets $25M in backing to help intelligence community deploy reliable AI agents

When it comes to matters of national security, it’s vitally important to ensure that the right intelligence gets to the right decision-makers, but doing this in today’s complex information technology environments is challenging, to say the least.

Enter the artificial intelligence startup Lumbra Inc., which has just raised $25 million in early-stage A funding to develop specialist autonomous agents tasked with sorting through the most sensitive data of all. Today’s Series A round was led by Point72 Ventures and Ansa Capital, with participation from seed round investor Costanoa.

Lumbra was founded last year by former Central Intelligence Agency officer Aaron Brown and ex-special forces infantry officer Michael Hiebert. Together, they’ve built a platform called LumbraOS, which is designed to orchestrate AI agents within high-consequence and ultra-secure computing environments, where risks of any kind simply cannot be tolerated.

Brown explained that LumbraOS was built from the ground up as a “model-neutral platform” that allows operators to mix and match various proprietary and open-weight AI models, assigning them different national security- and intelligence-related tasks. The platform is built on three key pillars: Nebula, StarChart and Astrolabe.

Nebula is the component tasked with managing agent orchestration, and works by tracing every “claim” generated by AI agents back to the primary source data behind that claim, so that domain experts can validate their outputs before decisions are made. StarChart is a dynamic knowledge graph that links disparate insights across multiple datasets through embedded sensitivity tags. Meanwhile, Astrolabe enforces governance policies and continuously evaluates each agent after benchmarking their performance prior to deployment to monitor for any alarming behavior.

Traditional AI systems developers struggle for years to ensure they meet the most rigorous federal security standards, but Brown and Hiebert say they developed LumbraOS specifically for classified computing environments. Just two months after launching their platform, they quietly landed a multimillion-dollar contract with an unnamed U.S. intelligence agency, with their AI agents operating on a top-secret defense network within just six months.

Impressed with the startup’s technology, the Pentagon followed up by naming Lumbra as one of two companies that underpins its Agent Network project, and one of seven “pace-setting projects” within its broader AI Acceleration strategy.

Following this traction, Lumbra’s co-founders believe there is potential for LumbraOS to expand beyond the intelligence community. They’re targeting enterprises in high-stakes industries such as healthcare, finance and law, where sensitive data leaks are deal breakers.

Brown said most organizations in these industries only use autonomous agents for singular tasks, if at all. That’s because they lack the tools to make those agents controllable, transparent and reliable enough at large scale. With its traceable audit logs and strict governance controls, Lumbra thinks it can help organizations to deploy agents safely across their networks to automate more complex workloads.

“The organizations that get agents right will spend less time telling them what to do and more time deciding what they may touch and what their work must prove,” Brown said. “Thousands of agents working a question together can find an insight while there’s still time to act on it. Lumbra exists to give decision-makers an advantage at the moment of decision.”

To target the enterprise, Lumbra plans to use the funds from today’s round to expand its engineering and product development teams and accelerate its go-to-market operations.

Ansa Capital Managing Partner Marco DeMeireles said the problem of trust and verifiability is the biggest barrier to adoption for AI agents in high-stakes environments. “Lumbra has demonstrated its ability to bring these capabilities into production across some of the most demanding environments within the U.S. government,” he said. “We believe these same capabilities will become foundational to how the world’s most critical enterprises deploy AI.”

#5577. Christina Haack Says She Paid Off Her College Debt by ‘Hitting It Big’ on a Las Vegas Slot Machine

Real estate investor Christina Haack doesn’t mind proving people wrong, even if that includes her own mom.

The “Flip or Flop” shared the unlikely story of her student loan payoff, after experiencing a “full circle” moment during a recent trip to Las Vegas.

In an Oct. 29 Instagram post, the HGTV personality, 43, shared a collection of photos where she’s posed in front of a slot machine while enjoying a glass of her own brand of wine, Clé Cachée.

“Really come full circle since age 21,” she explained in the caption before adding that she “paid off” her “college debt by hitting it big” on a slot machine called “top dollar.”

Haack was proud to close the loop “22 years later,” by getting to enjoy her own champagne while playing her “fav” machine. She called the experience “priceless,” and joked: “My mom always told me no one actually wins in Las Vegas. Turns out mama’s not always right.”

Her boyfriend, Chris Larocca, left a cheeky comment under the post, writing, “Maybe you have a good luck charm now…” to which she replied, “Most definitely.”

Haack has previously shared that when she was attending San Diego State, she “never thought about being on TV” and instead thought she “wanted to be a sports agent like Jerry Maguire.”

Eventually she realized she’d rather get her real estate license, and explained that she “got started in real estate at 21”—the same year she won big at a casino.

While Haack’s previous financial win may have been the luck of the draw, it’s safe to say her family is set up for success in a much more intentional way these days.

The mom-of-three recently made a splash online when she, her ex-husband Tarek El Moussa, and his new wife, Heather El Moussa, gifted daughter, Taylor El Moussa, a very expensive vehicle for her 16th birthday.

The close-knit crew of co-parents splurged on a $150,000 BMW X5, a lavish gift they said was “well deserved.”

“It’s such a beauty. I’m so happy for her,” Christina said in an Aug. 13 Instagram Reel that showcased the moment the teen was surprised with the new car, which had an enormous pink bow on it.

Heather wrote that the trio had worked together to surprise Taylor, and even joked that she was unsure if the car was more impressive, or if “the fact that three of us actually pulled this off” was a more jaw-dropping feat.

Tarek later shared more details about the purchase, explaining that the family had “good reason” to purchase the luxury vehicle during an appearance on the “Money Rehab” podcast with Nicole Lapin.

“She’s got a 4.2 GPA. She was MVP of her freshman soccer team. She’s an absolutely fantastic kid, and she didn’t just get it—she actually earned it,” he said. “If you ask me, she deserved it because she worked really, really hard.”

Noting that the car was also selected for its host of safety features, Tarek added that the vehicle was mostly his choice, as Taylor would have probably preferred a much-less-expensive Ford Bronco.

“Here’s the truth. She was flying in private jets when she was like, 1 year old,” he said. “So this kid has grown up around things. When I grew up, I didn’t have anything, right? So I’m obsessed with things because I never had things. She’s always had things.”

Staying firm in his belief that the gift was a “reward for all the work she’s done,” Tarek revealed that the family has also set her up for success financially in addition to showering her with pricey gifts.

Tarek noted that he has snapped up stocks and investment real estate for his teen daughter, and said that “if she were going to be a spoiled brat, she probably wouldn’t have got the 4.2 GPA, she probably wouldn’t have been MVP of her soccer team, and she probably wouldn’t have done the extra coaching.”

#5576. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5575. The 2027 Paint Colors of the Year Take an Emotional Turn

In the past, one hue typically dominated paint colors of the year, with different brands interpreting the color. For 2027, while there are a few blues and greens on offer, there is a much wider variety. Themes are less color-specific and more about emotional intent.

“Color has always been tied to emotion. We instinctively use it to create spaces that make us feel a certain way, and the colors we choose often reflect what we’re looking for in our lives,” says Lisbeth Parada, color marketing manager for Dutch Boy and Minwax brands.

​In 2027, that’s digital detox, permission to be authentic, and the opportunity for stillness and reflection.

​“We’re living in a world increasingly shaped by technology, algorithms, and an almost constant stream of information telling us what to think, what to buy, and how to live. We sense a growing desire to reconnect with our own instincts and the tangible experiences that make us feel human,” says Phillipa Radon, interior designer and C2 paint color specialist.

This year’s color trends tell us it’s not enough to treat home as a retreat anymore; recharging is necessary too, to manage the fast pace of the world around us. The variety of colors suggests multiple ways to gather that energy, with consumers choosing what resonates with them.

In new-construction homes, color choice is even more important, with paint offering homeowners a powerful way to personalize a brand-new space and forge that emotional connection to restoration.

​Here are the paint colors of the year for 2027.

​Sometimes paint color names are intentionally vague as part of their marketing micro-story. Not BEHR’s Grounded, with a name and a mossy green color that instantly frame the experience.

Its name has a double meaning too, as an invitation to breathe and get back to basics, amid digital overwhelm.

“What makes Grounded so relevant as BEHR’s 2027 Color of the Year is the way it balances two things people increasingly want from their homes: calm, and a feeling of life,” says Kayla Kratz, head of color at BEHR.

She notes that for many years, that meant paring down to a minimalist aesthetic, but today’s homeowners want more warmth and personality.

“Grounded answers that shift. The moss and olive tones bring a natural vitality, while warm brown undertones add depth and steadiness. The result is restorative without being static.”

Kratz says that the color replicates the dynamic greens of a forest, evolving throughout the day and changing light conditions.

​Deep Rooted, a nature-inspired warm orange, is energetic but steady and reassuring.

​“There’s an optimistic quality to the color. It has enough richness and energy to support bold contrasts and individual expression. The name brings those ideas together: feeling rooted while remaining open to possibility, and Deep Rooted captures that balance,” says Parada.

​It’s a perfect example of how paint color names are shaping the experience this year, with this color meant to encourage strength by standing still, not always easily done in today’s fast pace of living.

“​The paint color name captures both the color’s connection to nature and the sense of grounding many people want their homes to provide. At home, that translates into spaces that feel personal, welcoming, and comfortably lived in,” says Parada.

​Artifact is a smoky, atmospheric blue intended to create space to pause, recalibrate, and think more clearly after you’ve had a chance to catch your breath. These moments in time are both treasured and rare, which is reflected in the paint color name.

Artifact also embraces the idea of authorship, and how major change doesn’t necessarily require a makeover.

​“As consumers move away from creating homes that look like everyone else’s, they’re focusing on spaces that reflect who they are, where they’ve been, and what matters most to them, “ says Ashley McCollum, color marketing manager at Glidden.

​“People don’t necessarily want to reinvent themselves or start from scratch but rather make thoughtful adjustments that help their life feel more balanced and manageable,” says McCollum.

​“Artifact is not a reinvention, but a readjustment. It brings a sense of ease and relaxation after a busy day, helping you to unwind and feel more grounded. As a mid-tone, smoky blue, it leans warmer and has depth that strikes a balance between focus and comfort.”

This calming blue is nuanced and versatile, the kind of color that’s felt before it is seen, making it a good choice for homeowners who are choosing colors for an emotional impact.

Celery is a light green with yellow undertones that feels more herbal than botanical. It’s fresh and lively, marking a transition for Sherwin-Williams’ color trends.

Their paint color of the year last year was Universal Khaki, inspired by nostalgia and the comfort found in familiarity. Celery takes that feel-good energy into the future on a positive note. The color emerges alongside consumers’ appetite for expressive colors and a continued focus on wellness design.

A few paint colors of the year for 2027 are green, a carryover from last year’s color trends, but Celery offers a different perspective.

“While deeper, earthier greens have helped create grounded, restorative spaces, we’re beginning to see that nature-inspired palette evolve in a more expressive and optimistic direction,” says Ashley Banbury, color market manager at Sherwin-Williams.

“Celery reflects this shift, bringing a lighter, more playful energy to a color family that homeowners already know and love. It shows that green can be both calming and invigorating, offering a fresh perspective on nature-inspired design while encouraging homeowners to embrace color in more personal and unexpected ways,” says Banbury.

C2’s Pueblo is one of the more dynamic colors this year, with its identity shaped by an intentional refusal to commit to a single hue.

“What makes Pueblo so fascinating is that it resists a single definition. At its heart, it’s a warm, muted rose that bridges the space between deep floral tones and earthy neutrals. Its nuanced undertones interact with the changing temperature and intensity of natural light, revealing different aspects of the color throughout the day,” says Radon.

​“That complexity brings an unusual sense of dimension to an interior. Rather than creating a static backdrop, Pueblo becomes part of the experience of living in a space.”

​In the context of this year’s color themes, Pueblo taps into the idea that creativity and movement create energy to digitally detox.

​“There’s a certain confidence in choosing a color like that. It suggests we’re ready to move beyond simply creating a sanctuary and begin using our homes as places for creativity, individuality, and renewed engagement with life,” Radon says.

​Benjamin Moore has gone all-in on timeless over trends this year with their choice of Webster Green, a classic forest green that the paint brand is betting has staying power, given how prevalent various shades of green have been in color trends over the last few years.

​Green is adaptable and inherently energizing, which makes this shade a relevant tool for homeowners who want something sturdy but stylish too. Timeless design and decor choices are becoming more important to homeowners, for the sake of affordability and sustainability too.

​“Webster Green reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected, and continually new,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, at Benjamin Moore.​

​A sultry brown with plum undertones, French Press Coffee is all about striking the right mood and elevating daily rituals, another approach to gathering energy ahead of the daily grind. It’s the color equivalent to providing time and space to savor a hot, highly flavorful cup of coffee.

​It’s a little more nuanced than some of the other moody hues released in years prior, thanks to multidimensional color that adds visual weight and interest, while broadening potential applications.

​”French Press Coffee is the kind of color that reveals itself gradually,” said Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards. “As light shifts throughout the day, its subtle plum undertone emerges, adding complexity you don’t always see in a neutral. It’s grounding and restrained yet full of character.”

Blues dominated 2023’s colors of the year for their spa-inspired calm, and Valspar is rekindling those vibes. Chosen for being familiar but fresh, Cottage Door is a mid-toned blue with warm undertones.

Sue Kim, director of color marketing at Valspar, says that the color, “is reflective and warm, with timeless appeal that feels personal and grounding. Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortlessly into the home. It creates spaces that feel balanced, comforting, and inviting.”

The color taps into consumers’ increasingly pragmatic view on home design, and the company touts it as “designed for real life.” Homeowners would rather choose a color that endures than redecorate tomorrow.
